articles.title: Five Palaces, One Model: Testing Google’s Gemini 4 Hydrogen in AI Studio
articles.description: Last week Google shipped Gemini 4 Hydrogen, and within hours my X timeline was nothing but 3D scenes,...
articles.body_html:
Last week Google shipped Gemini 4 Hydrogen, and within hours my X timeline was nothing but 3D scenes, animations and generative art built from a single prompt. I couldn't just scroll past it, so I opened a browser tab and started building.

The result is Imperial Palaces: an interactive 3D world with five hand-coded (well, Hydrogen-coded) palaces, five camera views, a golden-hour/moonlit lighting switch, falling petals you can turn up to a blizzard, a synthesized koto soundtrack, and a one-click PNG snapshot.

👉 Live demo: palaces-eight.vercel.app
👉 Source: github.com/amananandrai/Palaces

What is Gemini 4 Hydrogen?

Quick context if you missed the launch. Hydrogen is the fast, cheaper tier of the Gemini 4 family. It sits next to the heavier Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon models and replaces the old "Flash" branding.

  • Launched: November 12, 2026
  • Built for: everyday coding and agentic workflows
  • Speed: Google says it finishes tasks about 2.5× faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash
  • Context: 1M-token context window, with four thinking levels (low, medium, high (the default) and a new xhigh)
  • Where to use it: Gemini app, Google Search, Google AI Studio, the Gemini API and Antigravity
  • API pricing: $1.50 per 1M input tokens and $7.50 per 1M output tokens

Here's the official announcement:

The inspiration: X went wild

What got me to open AI Studio wasn't the benchmark chart. It was the stuff people were making.

A code-based painting. Vamsi Batchu shared artwork that looks hand-painted but is pure single-file code: no external libraries, no image generators and no embedded assets. He gave Hydrogen a reference image and asked for a range of subjects in that painterly, gouache-like style.

Hydrogen vs. 3.8 Flash on the same 3D scene. Google itself boosted this one: the same animated 3D desert ranch prompt run on both models, with Hydrogen bringing the scene to life in under a minute.

A 3D city on an open book. This one came from before launch, while Hydrogen was being tested anonymously on Arena. Pankaj Kumar asked it for a 3D city sitting on an open book, and the whole site was generated in under 4 minutes.

And if you want the full firehose, Min Choi's roundup threads are a great rabbit hole:

Attempt #1: the Gemini app (didn't go well)

My first move was the obvious one: open the Gemini app and describe the scene I wanted, a Japanese Edo-era castle in a sakura garden.

The results weren't close to what I was seeing on X. The scenes were flatter and less detailed, and iterating on them felt clunky. Part of the reason is that free users in the Gemini app get Hydrogen through automatic model selection, so you don't always know which model is answering. The app is also built for chat, not for iterating on a multi-file 3D project.

Attempt #2: Google AI Studio (this is where it clicked)

So I moved to Google AI Studio, picked Gemini 4 Hydrogen explicitly, and used its app-building mode. That changed everything:

  • I knew exactly which model and thinking level I was using.
  • The output was a real React + TypeScript + Three.js + Vite project, not a single blob of HTML.
  • I could preview it live and keep refining in place.

From one castle to five palaces

The first good version was just the Edo Sanctuary: a multi-tiered castle keep, cherry trees, an arched red taiko-bashi bridge over a stream, stone lanterns, a koi pond and a sunset mountain backdrop. From there I refined it over a few rounds:

  1. Camera presets. Instead of only free-orbiting, I asked for curated views that fly the camera smoothly to the pond, the bridge, the palace and the horizon.
  2. Time of day. A Golden Hour / Moonlit Night toggle that blends the sun, sky, hemisphere light and water reflections instead of hard-cutting.
  3. Atmosphere controls. Calm / Breeze / Flurry petal density (240 → 640 → 1,200 particles) plus a wind-strength slider.
  4. Sound. An ambient soundscape made entirely with the Web Audio API.
  5. Snapshot. Export the current view as a PNG.
  6. More palaces. Russian, Victorian, Mughal and Persian scenes, each with its own bridge, water feature and particle type.

By the end the project was roughly 12,000 lines of TypeScript, and the codebase has no image or audio files to speak of: textures, geometry and sound are all generated in code.

The tour

Five camera views

The dock at the bottom has five presets. Pick one and the camera glides there; drag the scene and you're back to free orbit.

Grand Vista: the establishing shot shown at the top of this post.

Pond View: koi swimming under lily pads, with a wooden viewing pier in the corner.

Bridge View: the red taiko-bashi bridge over the stream.

Palace View: up close with the castle keep's tiered roofs and gold crests.

Horizon View: pulled back toward the mountains and the setting sun.

Breeze: petals and wind

Petal density has three levels, Calm, Breeze (the default) and Flurry, and the wind slider controls how hard the petals drift. Here it is on Flurry:

The particle type changes with each palace: sakura petals in Japan, snowfall in Russia, twilight motes at the Victorian manor and blossom or desert breezes in the Mughal and Persian scenes.

Moonlit Night

One click turns golden hour into a moonlit night. The sky goes deep indigo, the stars come out, the lanterns and windows glow warm, and the moon leaves a streak of light on the pond.

The pond at night is my favorite spot in the whole project:

Snapshot

The Snapshot button in the top right grabs the WebGL canvas with canvas.toDataURL('image/png') and downloads it as palace-<style>-<timeOfDay>.png. This is an untouched export straight from the button:

Five palaces

The top nav switches between five architectural styles, and each comes with its own setting:

Russian: Winter Terem Kremlin. Onion domes, a frozen rink, ice fishing, snowy pines and a granite bridge.

Victorian: Gothic Tudor Manor. A clock tower, a cast-iron arch bridge and a swan fountain lake.

Mughal: Diwan-i-Khas. White domes and chhatris, a stone bridge and an octagonal charbagh pool.

Persian: Safavid Desert Oasis. Turquoise tile domes, a triple-arch bridge, a qanat lagoon and palms.

Zen mode

Press H (or "Hide Controls") to slide the dock away and just enjoy the view.

Under the hood

A few things in the generated code impressed me:

  • Procedural textures. Stone, roof tiles, plaster, the namako lattice walls and hinoki wood are all painted at runtime onto CanvasTextures, with matching bump maps.
  • Instanced foliage. Blossoms, leaves, grass blades and cattails use THREE.InstancedMesh with per-instance colors, so thousands of petals stay smooth.
  • Synthesized audio. The ambient engine builds stream water and garden wind from filtered noise, and plays koto-style plucks on a D Hirajoshi pentatonic scale. There isn't a single audio file in it.
  • Smooth transitions. Camera presets and the day/night blend are lerped inside the render loop through refs, so React doesn't re-render every frame.

Stack: React 19 · TypeScript · Three.js · Vite · Tailwind CSS · lucide-react · deployed on Vercel.

What I learned

  1. The tool matters as much as the model. The same model gave me mediocre results in the chat app and great ones in AI Studio. Choosing the model explicitly and getting a real project structure made all the difference.
  2. Get a good v1, then iterate. Hydrogen is fast enough that "make the water reflect the moon" or "add four more palaces" turns into a quick loop instead of a big ask.
  3. The demos on X are real. I went in skeptical and came out with something I'm happy to share.

Go try it, flip to Moonlit Night, crank the petals to Flurry and take a snapshot:

🏯 palaces-eight.vercel.app

If you build something with Hydrogen, drop it in the comments. I'd love to see it! ⭐ The repo is here if you want to poke at the code.

articles.title: Matt Pocock's Agent Skills: The Markdown Files Everyone's Installing (and Whether They Still Matter)
articles.description: Quick confession: I rolled my eyes when "a folder of Markdown files" started topping GitHub trending....
articles.body_html:
Quick confession: I rolled my eyes when "a folder of Markdown files" started topping GitHub trending. Then I tried it, and I stopped rolling my eyes.

The folder is mattpocock/skills. Let's talk about who's behind it, why it blew up, what's inside, and whether it's still worth your time now that models keep getting smarter.

Wait, who is Matt Pocock?

Not an AI lab researcher, which is part of the charm. His path is a bit unusual:

  • Voice coach first. He came from performing arts and public speaking coaching, then taught himself to code.
  • XState and Stately. He was on the XState core team and a developer advocate at Stately, where he helped bring TypeScript into XState.
  • Vercel. He worked there as a developer advocate. By his own account he took the job as a safety net in case his course didn't work out.
  • Total TypeScript. It did work out. The course passed $2.5M in sales and he left Vercel to teach full time.
  • AI Hero. Launched in July 2025 as a course for web developers retraining as AI engineers, and it became his most successful launch so far.

He's also loud on X (roughly 250k followers), which explains some of the repo's reach.

So the skills come from a teacher who's spent years explaining hard things simply. You can feel that in the files.

The repo, by the numbers

Star counts depend on who you ask and when, so treat these as a rough timeline:

When (2026) What happened
Spring Hit #1 trending within a day and crossed ~22k stars on day one; ~45k by Apr 29, ~58k by May 4
Mid-May Topped GitHub's weekly trending with +1,618 stars
Late July Led the weekly trending list again with +10,651 stars
Early Sept #2 on daily trending, +2,206 stars in 24 hours, ~254k total
Latest trackers ~300k stars, ~27k forks

A few fun facts: it's MIT licensed, GitHub reports it as "Shell 100%" because there's no actual app code, and it has a tiny contributor list. It's basically a personal .claude directory published to the world.

skills.sh and the install counts

Stars are vanity. Installs are closer to usage. skills.sh is Vercel's directory and leaderboard for agent skills (npx skills add owner/repo, works with Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Copilot and friends). Pocock's skills dominate it. On the all-time board:

Skill All-time rank Installs
grill-me #3 1.6M
grill-with-docs #10 1.3M
grilling #16 1.1M
prototype #18 1.1M
triage #19 1.1M
domain-modeling #25 ~988K
code-review #58 ~900K
implement #61 ~873K

The repo also gets name-dropped in the usual awesome lists, like awesome-claude-code. And one dev who tried the heavier "Superpowers" skill pack wrote that they prefer the leaner grill-me and grill-with-docs, whose entry files are only about seven lines each.

(Install counts include some older skill names, since Pocock reorganizes things often.)

What's actually in it

About 27 skills, split into two kinds:

  • User-invoked: you type them (/grill-me). They orchestrate.
  • Model-invoked: the agent can reach for them when a task fits (tdd, code-review).

The README's rule: a user-invoked skill can call model-invoked ones, never another user-invoked one. Simple and predictable.

The README organizes the skills around four recurring ways agents let you down:

Agent problem Skills that fix it
Builds the wrong thing /grill-me, /grill-with-docs
Way too wordy /grill-with-docs (shared glossary)
Code doesn't work /tdd, /diagnosing-bugs
Codebase becomes spaghetti /to-spec, /improve-codebase-architecture

The skills that save you the most time (with examples)

/grill-me: stop the guessing

Give an agent a fuzzy request and it'll confidently build something. This skill flips it so the agent interviews you first, branch by branch, until the plan is solid.

/grill-me I want to add caching to our /products API

Expect questions like: how stale can data be? What invalidates an entry? Per-user or shared? What happens under a stampede? Ten minutes of questions beats one rejected implementation.

Use /grill-me for general plans and /grill-with-docs when you're inside a codebase.

CONTEXT.md: say one word instead of twenty

The README's point is that agents get dropped into a project and invent their own vocabulary, then burn tokens explaining things the long way. /grill-with-docs fixes that by building a glossary (CONTEXT.md) and decision records (docs/adr/) as you talk.

Say your team calls it a "booking", but the code has "reservation", "order" and "slot". The agent spots the clash, you pick "booking", and it's written down. Now names are consistent, the agent searches with the right term, and replies get shorter. That's a direct token saving.

/tdd and /diagnosing-bugs: give the agent a feedback loop

An agent with no failing test is flying blind. /tdd runs red-green-refactor, one thin vertical slice at a time:

/tdd Add a 10% discount for orders over $100

One failing test, minimum code to pass, tidy, next behavior. /diagnosing-bugs does the same for nasty bugs: reproduce, minimize, hypothesize, instrument, fix, add a regression test. No more "random edits and vibes".

Specs, tickets and parallel agents

  • /to-spec turns the conversation into a spec on your tracker.
  • /to-tickets splits it into small tickets with dependencies.
  • /implement builds it (using /tdd, and /code-review before commit).
  • /implement-spec runs parallel subagents over a task graph.
  • /wayfinder handles projects too big for one session.

Keeping context clean

  • /handoff condenses a long session into a doc a fresh agent can pick up.
  • /wait-what re-explains a confusing message in plain English.
  • /retro suggests improvements to your agent setup after a session.
  • /improve-codebase-architecture finds modules worth deepening and shows them in an HTML report. It surveys, it doesn't fix legacy messes for you.

Okay, but is it still relevant with newer models?

Fair question. Models improve every few months, and a lot of prompt tricks die fast. Here's my honest read:

Why it's holding up:

  • These skills are mostly process, not model workarounds. Clarifying requirements, shared vocabulary, tests and small slices help human teams too, and that doesn't expire when a model upgrades.
  • Pocock keeps updating the repo and uses it with current models. As of mid-2026 he said he was still mostly on Opus 4.8 and cautious about fully switching to the newest one, and a recent release added a wait-what skill aimed at Opus being wordy.
  • His AI Engineer Europe 2026 talk makes the argument directly: AI-assisted development leans on shared design concepts, precise domain language, fast feedback loops and humans owning the design.
  • The skills are tiny. A seven-line skill costs almost nothing in context, so there's little downside to keeping it.

Where I'd stay skeptical (this part is my opinion):

  • Some skills compensate for specific model habits (rambling, not asking questions). As models get better at that on their own, those skills may matter less.
  • Nobody has published rigorous benchmarks showing before/after gains. The evidence is installs, stars and user testimonials, which show popularity rather than proven efficiency.
  • A skill that fires too often can waste context. Install the ones you'll actually use, not all 27.

My take: treat it as a toolbox, not a religion. Start with /grill-me, add /tdd, and see what sticks.

Getting started in 60 seconds 

npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills

Pick your skills (include setup-matt-pocock-skills), then run /setup-matt-pocock-skills once per repo. Claude Code users can also use the plugin route:

claude plugin marketplace add mattpocock/skills
claude plugin install mattpocock-skills@mattpocock

Lost? Type /ask-matt and it'll point you to the right skill.

A simple loop: /grill-with-docs → /to-spec → /to-tickets → /implement → /handoff when the session gets long → /retro at the end.

Wrap-up

The magic isn't any single prompt. It's the habit: spend your human attention early (clarify the plan, agree on words), then give the agent tight feedback (tests, small slices, reviews). Do that and you get fewer retries, shorter answers and code you can reason about.

Try one skill this week. What's the one you'd install first?

articles.title: I Tried Respan Gateway: An Open-Source LLM Gateway Written in Rust
articles.description: If you've built anything on more than one LLM provider, you know the drill. OpenAI's SDK here,...
articles.body_html:
If you've built anything on more than one LLM provider, you know the drill. OpenAI's SDK here, Anthropic's there, a wrapper to make them look alike, and retry logic you wrote at 2am and don't fully trust. An LLM gateway is supposed to take that away: one endpoint, any model, and the plumbing handled for you.

Respan Gateway is a new open-source one, written in Rust and public since October. I installed it on my Windows PC, pointed it at Gemini, broke a provider on purpose, and checked whether it does what it says. Everything below is from that run: real commands, real timings, real screenshots.

What Respan Gateway is

Respan Gateway is a single binary that sits between your code and AI APIs. You point the SDK you already use (OpenAI, Anthropic or Gemini) at it, ask for any model, and it translates the request into whatever format that model's provider speaks.

What stood out before I ran it:

  • Everything is a plugin. Providers, routing, pricing, MCP and tracing are all built on the same public Rust API you can use to write your own.
  • 16 providers built in, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, xAI, DeepSeek, Mistral, Groq, OpenRouter, Ollama and vLLM, plus any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
  • MIT or Apache-2.0, self-hosted, free.
  • A built-in web UI with a live request log, a playground and a route debugger.

Installing it on Windows

Respan’s docs list four ways to install: pip install respan-gateway (which ships the compiled binary and covers Windows), cargo install, a release zip, or Docker. On a Linux box, the pip install took about 3 seconds.

My config

You can start with no config at all: export a provider key and run respan-gateway. For this test I wanted a fallback route I could break on purpose, so I wrote a small gateway.toml. It has Gemini as the real provider, plus a provider called down that points at a local port where nothing is listening:

[providers.gemini]

vendor = "gemini"

key    = "env:GEMINI_API_KEY"

# Nothing listens on port 9: this provider is "down" on purpose

[providers.down]

formats  = ["openai-chat"]

base_url = "http://127.0.0.1:9/v1"

# Any bare "gemini-*" model tries the dead provider first, then Gemini

[routes."gemini-*"]

to      = ["down/{model}", "gemini/{model}"]

tries   = 2

backoff = "200ms"

The key sits in a .env file next to the config, which the gateway reads on startup. Before starting, respan-gateway check validates the file and prints exactly what it will serve: providers, endpoints, routes and whether auth is on. That saved me a guess-and-restart loop. A note on the port: the gateway’s default is 8080. For my final run I started it with --listen 127.0.0.1:8081 because an earlier test was still using 8080, so my screenshots show 8081. The code in this article uses the default, 8080.

The same config shows up in the web UI, with secrets hidden:

One default I liked: with no client keys configured, the gateway only answers on loopback and refuses to start on a public address. You can't accidentally expose your provider keys by forgetting a setting.

Any SDK, any model

This is the headline feature, so I tested it first. I sent the same prompt to gemini/gemini-3.5-flash-lite twice: once in Anthropic Messages format (POST /v1/messages) and once in OpenAI Chat format (POST /v1/chat/completions). Both came back correct, in 1.03s and 1.52s.

The gateway turned the Anthropic-format request into a Gemini call and translated the answer back, including usage in Anthropic's shape (input_tokens, output_tokens). The request detail in the UI shows it plainly: format anthropic-messages, provider gemini.

The Playground makes this even more visible. I picked the Anthropic Messages API and a Gemini model, and the reply is labelled "served by gemini" and "translated from Anthropic Messages":

In code, that's the whole trick: keep your client, change the base URL, change the model string.

from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic(base_url="http://localhost:8080", api_key="unused")

reply = client.messages.create(

model="gemini/gemini-3.5-flash-lite",

max_tokens=1024,

messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "In one sentence, what does an LLM gateway do?"}],

)

Two things I ran into on the way, neither the gateway's fault:

  • Google retired a model under me. My first pick, gemini-2.5-flash, is closed to new users. The gateway passed Google's own 404 message straight through, so it was obvious what to change.
  • Thinking tokens eat small budgets. With full Gemini 3.5 Flash and max_tokens=150, the model spent 140 tokens thinking and returned a cut-off answer. The gateway reported it honestly in the usage (thinking_tokens: 140). Raising the budget and using Flash Lite fixed it, and replies dropped to around a second.

Fallback: breaking a provider on purpose

Here's the test I cared most about. I asked for the bare model name gemini-3.5-flash-lite, which matches the gemini-* route. The gateway tries down first, fails, retries, then falls back to Gemini. I ran it three times:

Every call came back 200 with the right answer. The client never saw a failure. The interesting part is call 3: after four failures, the gateway put down on cooldown and skipped it, so the request went straight to Gemini in 0.79s.

The first two calls took about 5 seconds each. Most of that is likely Windows retrying the connection to a dead local port before giving up, with tries = 2 doubling it. A provider that answers with a fast error would fail over much quicker. Either way, it's worth tuning tries and backoff for your setup.

The gateway's own log tells the same story. The third line shows the bare model name routed to gemini:

)

My favourite debugging feature is on the Routes page. Type a model name into "Try a model" and it shows where the request would go and why. Here it shows down at 100% errors and Gemini at 682 ms, without sending anything:

The detail view for one of the failed-over requests shows the whole 4.97s and that gemini served it:

Routes can do more than plain fallback. They can pick cheapest, fastest, weighted or random, hedge a slow call against a second provider (hedge = "200ms"), filter with needs = ["tools"], and match globs like the one I used. Config changes reload without a restart (--watch or SIGHUP).

The web UI

Open http://localhost:8080/ui/ and you get a proper dashboard, not an afterthought. After my clean run: 5 requests, 0% errors, tokens in and out, and per-provider stats.

The Requests page is a live log with model, endpoint, provider, status, latency and tokens for every call, plus filters and export:

Providers shows each upstream, what it serves and the formats it speaks:

Models lists all 57 models my Gemini key could reach, with context windows:

Notice the empty Price / M column. The gateway only knows a price when the provider's model list includes one or you declare it, and Gemini's doesn't. So out of the box I got tokens but no dollar figures for Gemini. You can fix that with a few lines per model:

[models."gemini/gemini-3.5-flash-lite"]

pricing = { input = 0.30, output = 2.50 }   # $ per million tokens, Google's list price (Nov 2026)

Gateway-side MCP

I didn't test this one, but it's unusual enough to mention. You can put MCP servers or built-in tool vendors (web search, browsers, code sandboxes, memory) behind the gateway, and it runs the tools inside the chat request. A plain chat client that has never heard of MCP can still use them.

Performance

Performance is Respan's main pitch. These are their published numbers from the README:

Two caveats, to be fair. These are Respan's own benchmarks, and LiteLLM was run with a single worker, so scaling its workers narrows the gap. I didn't run a load test. What I can say is that the gateway added nothing I could notice: my round trips were dominated by Gemini itself.

What I didn't love

  • It's young. v0.3.0 at the time of writing. Expect a smaller provider list, plugin ecosystem and community than LiteLLM's for a while.
  • No prices for Gemini out of the box. The request log shows tokens but not dollars until you declare pricing.
  • Failed attempts are invisible on the Providers page. down shows 0 requests there, while the Routes page correctly shows it at 100% errors. The Routes page is where to look.
  • Custom plugins mean Rust. The plugin API is clean (one trait, four hooks), but a Python-only team is limited to config and the built-ins.
  • The docs are thin in places. The useful routing details (pick, tries, hedge) live in docs/configuration.md and gateway.example.toml in the repo. Read those first.

Who should use it

Respan Gateway makes the most sense if you want a self-hosted gateway that's light on latency and memory, you like having routing and fallbacks in one readable TOML file, and you want to mix SDKs and providers without rewriting client code.

If you need the widest list of integrations today, or a mature enterprise feature set, LiteLLM is still the safer bet for now.

For me, the parts that matter worked exactly as described on a real provider. Anthropic-format requests came back from Gemini, a dead provider was routed around and then put on cooldown, and check plus the Routes page made it easy to see what the gateway was doing and why. That's more than I expect from a v0.3.

articles.title: Hardening Kotlin APIs with OAuth2 and JSON Web Tokens
articles.description: I read this article and I rewrite it in my own words.   A guide to implementing delegated...
articles.body_html:
I read this article and I rewrite it in my own words.

A guide to implementing delegated authorization and stateless authentication in modern backend services.

The Shift Toward Defensive API Design

API security stopped being a bolt-on feature the moment microservices became the default architecture. When a single user request triggers a cascade of calls across five different services, traditional session-based authentication collapses under the weight of database lookups and state synchronization. Kotlin has emerged as a preferred language for building these backends, largely because its type system and coroutine support allow for expressive, safe security configurations.

Modern security relies on two primary pillars: OAuth2 for authorization and JSON Web Tokens (JWT) for authentication. While beginners often conflate the two, they serve distinct purposes. OAuth2 defines how a user grants a third-party application access to their data without handing over their password. JWT provides the mechanism for encoding that access into a portable, verifiable format. Organizations like JetBrains emphasize that securing APIs for beginners requires moving away from local JSESSIONID cookies toward token-based flows that work across mobile apps, web frontends, and server-to-server communication.

In the Kotlin ecosystem, the choice often lands between Spring Security and Ktor. Spring Security provides a mature, albeit complex, framework for enterprise-grade protection, while Ktor offers a lightweight, DSL-driven approach. Regardless of the framework, the goal remains the same: ensure that every incoming request is authenticated (identifying who the user is) and authorized (verifying what they are allowed to do) without introducing a single point of failure or an unnecessary performance bottleneck.

OAuth2: The Delegated Authorization Framework

OAuth2 is not an authentication protocol; it is an authorization framework. It solves the "password sharing" problem by introducing an intermediary—the Authorization Server. In a typical Kotlin backend, the application assumes the role of a Resource Server, protecting data on behalf of the user.

According to the OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework (RFC 6749), the system relies on four distinct roles working in concert:

┌──────────────┐          ┌──────────────────────┐
│ Resource     │  (A)     │                      │
│ Owner (User) │ ────────▶│    Client App        │
└──────────────┘          │ (Mobile/Web/Server)  │
       ▲                  └──────────────────────┘
       │                             │
       │ (B) Grant                   │ (C) Access Token
       ▼                             ▼
┌──────────────┐          ┌──────────────────────┐
│ Authorization│          │   Resource Server    │
│ Server       │          │   (Kotlin API)       │
└──────────────┘          └──────────────────────┘

For most Kotlin developers, the Authorization Code Flow is the standard. The client redirects the user to an identity provider (like Keycloak, Auth0, or Google). After the user logs in, the provider sends a temporary code back to the client. The client then exchanges this code for an access_token. Spring Security's OAuth2 support automates much of this handshake, allowing developers to focus on defining protected endpoints rather than managing the low-level HTTP redirects.

By delegating the login process to a specialized server, you reduce the attack surface of your own application. You don't store passwords, manage password resets, or handle multi-factor authentication (MFA) logic. You simply trust the tokens issued by the Authorization Server, provided they meet your validation criteria.

Anatomy of a JSON Web Token

If OAuth2 is the process, the JSON Web Token (JWT) is the artifact. A JWT is a compact, URL-safe string representing claims to be transferred between two parties. Its primary advantage is that it is self-contained. All the necessary user data—their ID, roles, and the token expiration—is encoded directly in the string.

A JWT consists of three parts separated by dots: the Header, the Payload, and the Signature.

  1. Header: Specifies the algorithm used for signing (e.g., HS256 or RS256).
  2. Payload: Contains the "claims." These are statements about the user and additional data like iat (issued at) and exp (expiration time).
  3. Signature: Created by hashing the header and payload with a secret key. This ensures the token hasn't been tampered with.

Ktor's JWT implementation allows you to verify these signatures using either a shared secret or a public/private key pair. In a production environment, RS256 (Asymmetric) is preferred. The Authorization Server signs the token with a private key, and your Kotlin API verifies it using a public key.

// Example of a JWT payload structure
{
  "sub": "1234567890",
  "name": "Jane Doe",
  "admin": true,
  "iat": 1516239022,
  "exp": 1516242622
}

Because the token is signed, the Resource Server can trust the admin: true claim without querying a database on every request. This enables stateless authentication, where the server doesn't need to store session data in memory or a cache like Redis. However, this carries a trade-off: tokens are difficult to revoke before they expire. If a token is stolen, the attacker has access until the exp timestamp is reached. This makes short-lived tokens and refresh token patterns mandatory for any secure implementation.

Implementing Security in the Kotlin Ecosystem

When moving from theory to code, Kotlin developers generally choose between the Spring Boot ecosystem and the Ktor framework. Each offers distinct patterns for integrating OAuth2 and JWT.

Spring Boot and Spring Security

Spring Boot provides extensive auto-configuration. By adding the spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server dependency, you can configure your application to validate JWTs by simply pointing to an issuer URI. Baeldung’s guide on Spring Security OAuth JWT notes that you can even include custom claims in the token to pass domain-specific data, such as a subscription tier or a tenant ID.

@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
class SecurityConfig {
    @Bean
    fun filterChain(http: HttpSecurity): SecurityFilterChain {
        http
            .authorizeHttpRequests { auth ->
                auth.requestMatchers("/api/public/**").permitAll()
                    .anyRequest().authenticated()
            }
            .oauth2ResourceServer { oauth2 ->
                oauth2.jwt { jwt ->
                    // Configure JWT validation here
                }
            }
        return http.build()
    }
}

Ktor Server

Ktor takes a more explicit approach using its Authentication plugin. As detailed in the Ktor Authentication documentation, you install the JWT provider and define how to validate the credentials. This is often more idiomatic for Kotlin developers who prefer a functional style over Spring's annotation-heavy architecture.

install(Authentication) {
    jwt("auth-jwt") {
        realm = "my-api"
        verifier(makeJwtVerifier(issuer, audience))
        validate { credential ->
            if (credential.payload.getClaim("username").asString() != "") {
                JWTPrincipal(credential.payload)
            } else {
                null
            }
        }
    }
}

For teams that want to avoid the overhead of a dedicated Authorization Server like Keycloak, it is possible to implement stateless JWT authentication manually, where the API itself issues and validates tokens. This is often suitable for smaller projects where vendor lock-in or the cost of SaaS identity providers is a concern.

Security Best Practices and Common Pitfalls

Implementing the protocols is only half the battle; configuring them securely is where most vulnerabilities arise. One of the most frequent mistakes is using weak signing keys. For HS256, the secret should be a high-entropy string of at least 256 bits. For RS256, generating a proper Java KeyStore (JKS) ensures that your private keys are stored securely and not hardcoded in application properties.

Token Expiration and Refreshing
Never issue access tokens with long lifespans. A standard practice is 15 minutes for an access token, paired with a longer-lived refresh token stored in an HttpOnly, Secure cookie. This limits the window of opportunity for an attacker if a token is intercepted. Software Patterns Lexicon highlights that token validation must include checks for the nbf (not before) and iat (issued at) claims to prevent replay attacks.

Algorithm Verification
A classic JWT vulnerability involves the "alg": "none" attack, where an attacker modifies the header to disable signature verification. Modern libraries like java-jwt or Spring Security's NimbusJwtDecoder protect against this by default, but you must explicitly define the expected algorithm during the verification phase.

Scope vs. Role
In OAuth2, scopes represent what the application is allowed to do (e.g., read:profile), while roles represent what the user is allowed to do (e.g., ROLE_ADMIN). Mixing these up leads to over-privileged applications. Always validate both the presence of the correct scope and the user's roles before granting access to sensitive data.

Finally, monitor your logs for frequent 401 Unauthorized or 403 Forbidden errors. While these are often benign user errors, a sudden spike can indicate a brute-force attempt or a misconfigured client attempting to use an expired refresh token. Security is a moving target, and in the Kotlin ecosystem, staying updated with the latest Ktor OAuth features or Spring Boot releases is the best defense against emerging threats.

  2. The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework — The definitive specification for OAuth2 roles and flows.
  3. OAuth2 :: Spring Security — Official documentation for integrating OAuth2 into Spring-based Kotlin applications.
  4. JSON Web Tokens | Ktor Documentation — Reference for handling JWT authentication within the Ktor framework.
  5. Using JWT with Spring Security OAuth | Baeldung — Technical guide covering custom claims and keystore management.
  6. Authentication and authorization in Ktor Server — Overview of the Ktor Authentication plugin and its supported schemes.
  7. Stateless JWT Authentication with Spring Security — Explores implementing JWT without a dedicated authorization server.
  8. OAuth2 and JWT in Kotlin: Secure Authentication and Token Management — Discusses design patterns for token validation and refresh mechanisms.
  9. OAuth | Ktor Documentation — Details on configuring external OAuth providers in Ktor.

articles.title: TypeScript `protected` vs `private` in 2026: The Inheritance Visibility Rules That Bite Teams Mid-Refactor
articles.description: TypeScript's protected and private modifiers look similar but enforce wildly different visibility rules during inheritance. Teams hit these constraints mid-refactor when subclass access patterns suddenly break type checking.
articles.body_html:
TypeScript protected vs private in 2026: The Inheritance Visibility Rules That Bite Teams Mid-Refactor

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

The Access Modifier Confusion That Breaks Refactors

Teams discover the difference between protected and private when a seemingly safe refactor suddenly fails type checking. A developer extracts shared logic into a base class, marks a field private, and watches the entire subclass hierarchy reject access to that field. The build breaks. The refactor stalls. The team backtracks to public and ships the leaky abstraction.

The problem: private members vanish the moment inheritance enters the picture. Subclasses cannot touch them. The TypeScript compiler enforces this boundary strictly, treating private as a hard contract between the declaring class and no one else. When developers expect inheritance-friendly visibility, they reach for the wrong modifier and hit a wall mid-refactor.

Problem diagram showing private field blocking subclass access

The solution: protected members expose themselves to the inheritance chain. Subclasses gain access. The refactor proceeds without visibility violations. The type checker passes because the modifier matches the actual access pattern.

Solution diagram showing protected field allowing subclass access

This matters because the wrong choice compounds during maintenance. A private field that should have been protected forces awkward workarounds (public getters, reflection tricks, or abandoning inheritance entirely). Teams that understand the visibility rules ship cleaner hierarchies and avoid the mid-refactor panic when TypeScript refuses to compile.

Key Takeaways

  • private members are invisible to subclasses; only the declaring class can access them, making them unsuitable for inheritance-based patterns.
  • protected members expose themselves to the entire inheritance chain, allowing subclasses to access and override them while still hiding them from external code.
  • TypeScript's structural typing treats private as a nominal constraint: two classes with identically named private fields are incompatible even if their shapes match.
  • Both private and protected disappear during compilation to JavaScript; the runtime offers zero enforcement, making these purely compile-time contracts.
  • Choosing the wrong modifier mid-refactor forces visibility violations that break builds and require either exposing fields as public or redesigning the hierarchy.

How protected and private Actually Work: The Visibility Rules

TypeScript's access modifiers control compile-time visibility, not runtime behavior. The TypeScript handbook defines three visibility levels: public (accessible everywhere, the default), protected (accessible within the class and its subclasses), and private (accessible only within the declaring class). These boundaries exist solely during type checking.

A private member creates a one-class perimeter. The declaring class can read and write it. Subclasses cannot. External code cannot. The TypeScript compiler enforces this by rejecting any access outside the declaring class:

class DatabaseConnection {
  private credentials: string;

  constructor(creds: string) {
    this.credentials = creds; // ✓ allowed in declaring class
  }

  connect() {
    console.log(`Connecting with ${this.credentials}`);
  }
}

class SecureConnection extends DatabaseConnection {
  audit() {
    console.log(this.credentials); // ✗ Property 'credentials' is private
  }
}

The subclass SecureConnection inherits the structure of DatabaseConnection, but the private modifier blocks access. The compiler sees the reference to this.credentials and rejects it. The error message is explicit: Property 'credentials' is private and only accessible within class 'DatabaseConnection'.

A protected member expands the perimeter to include the inheritance chain. The declaring class and all subclasses can access it. External code still cannot. This matches the common pattern where base classes define fields that subclasses need to implement specialized behavior:

class Cache {
  protected storage: Map<string, unknown>;

  constructor() {
    this.storage = new Map(); // ✓ allowed in declaring class
  }

  get(key: string): unknown {
    return this.storage.get(key); // ✓ allowed in declaring class
  }
}

class LRUCache extends Cache {
  private accessOrder: string[] = [];

  get(key: string): unknown {
    const value = this.storage.get(key); // ✓ allowed in subclass
    this.accessOrder.push(key);
    return value;
  }
}

The protected field storage is visible to both Cache and LRUCache. The subclass can directly read the map to implement custom eviction logic. The external API remains unchanged because protected still hides the field from consumers of the class.

TypeScript visibility diagram showing access modifier boundaries

TypeScript does not allow cross-hierarchy protected access. A subclass can access protected members on this, but not on sibling class instances. This prevents a Derived1 instance from reaching into a Derived2 instance's protected state, even though both extend the same base class. The TypeScript handbook explains this as a safeguard against unintended coupling between unrelated subclasses.

The visibility rules create a hierarchy of access: private locks the field to one class, protected extends visibility to descendants, and public removes restrictions entirely. Developers choose based on how the field participates in inheritance.

The Structural Typing Trap: Why private Members Break Type Compatibility

TypeScript uses structural typing for most type checks. Two objects with identical shapes are compatible, regardless of where they were declared. The compiler compares properties, not names or origins. A { x: number } from one file matches a { x: number } from another.

private and protected members break this rule. The TypeScript compiler treats them nominally: two types are compatible only if their private or protected members come from the same declaration. The TypeScript handbook states this explicitly: "For two types to be considered compatible, if one of them has a private member, then the other must have a private member that originated in the same declaration."

This creates surprising incompatibility between structurally identical classes:

class Animal {
  private name: string;
  constructor(name: string) {
    this.name = name;
  }
}

class Employee {
  private name: string;
  constructor(name: string) {
    this.name = name;
  }
}

const animal: Animal = new Animal("Dog");
const employee: Employee = new Employee("Alice");

const entity: Animal = employee; // ✗ Type 'Employee' is not assignable to type 'Animal'

Both Animal and Employee have a private name: string field. The shapes are identical. Structural typing would treat them as compatible. The compiler rejects the assignment because the private members originated in different declarations. The name in Animal and the name in Employee are distinct, incompatible types.

Inheritance preserves the declaration origin. A subclass that extends a base class inherits the base's private and protected members, including their declaration origin. This makes the subclass compatible with the base:

class Animal {
  private name: string;
  constructor(name: string) {
    this.name = name;
  }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
  constructor(name: string) {
    super(name);
  }
}

const animal: Animal = new Dog("Rex"); // ✓ compatible via inheritance

The private name in Dog originated in Animal. The compiler sees the shared origin and allows the assignment. This nominal check ensures that private members remain truly private: only classes in the same inheritance chain can share them.

This matters during refactors. Extracting a base class with private fields breaks compatibility with any external code that expects the original type. The structural shape remains identical, but the declaration origin changes. Type checks that previously passed now fail.

The workaround: use protected for fields that participate in inheritance, or avoid access modifiers entirely for fields that need structural compatibility.

protected vs private in Inheritance Hierarchies: Real Refactoring Scenarios

Teams hit the protected versus private decision when pulling shared state into a base class. The question: should subclasses access this field directly, or only through methods?

A common scenario: multiple service classes share database connection logic. The initial implementation duplicates the connection field in each class. The refactor extracts a BaseService with the shared connection. The developer marks it private to enforce encapsulation:

class BaseService {
  private connection: DatabaseConnection;

  constructor(conn: DatabaseConnection) {
    this.connection = conn;
  }

  protected query(sql: string): Promise<unknown[]> {
    return this.connection.execute(sql);
  }
}

class UserService extends BaseService {
  async findById(id: number): Promise<User | null> {
    // Must use this.query() instead of direct connection access
    const rows = await this.query(`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${id}`);
    return rows[0] as User;
  }
}

The private connection forces subclasses to use the protected query() method. This works when the base class API covers all use cases. It breaks when a subclass needs direct connection access for transaction management, connection pooling, or custom query building. The refactor stalls. The developer either exposes connection as public (leaking the abstraction) or redesigns the base class API to support every possible use case (overengineering).

The alternative: mark connection as protected. Subclasses gain direct access. The base class still hides it from external code:

class BaseService {
  protected connection: DatabaseConnection;

  constructor(conn: DatabaseConnection) {
    this.connection = conn;
  }
}

class TransactionalUserService extends BaseService {
  async createWithAudit(user: User): Promise<void> {
    const tx = await this.connection.beginTransaction(); // ✓ direct access
    try {
      await tx.execute("INSERT INTO users ...");
      await tx.execute("INSERT INTO audit_log ...");
      await tx.commit();
    } catch (error) {
      await tx.rollback();
      throw error;
    }
  }
}

The subclass uses the connection directly for transaction control. The base class does not need to anticipate every transaction pattern. The protected modifier trusts subclasses to use the connection correctly.

Inheritance hierarchy showing protected field access patterns

Another scenario: a Component base class manages lifecycle state. Subclasses need to read the current state to decide whether to run certain logic. The developer marks state private and adds a getter:

class Component {
  private state: "mounted" | "unmounted" = "unmounted";

  mount() {
    this.state = "mounted";
    this.onMount();
  }

  protected onMount() {
    // hook for subclasses
  }

  isMounted(): boolean {
    return this.state === "mounted";
  }
}

class AsyncComponent extends Component {
  protected onMount() {
    if (this.isMounted()) { // must call getter
      this.loadData();
    }
  }
}

The getter works, but adds indirection. Every subclass that checks state calls isMounted() instead of reading state directly. If the state shape becomes more complex (adding "mounting", "unmounting", "error" states), the base class must add corresponding getters for each state. This scales poorly.

The protected alternative eliminates the getter:

class Component {
  protected state: "mounted" | "unmounted" = "unmounted";

  mount() {
    this.state = "mounted";
    this.onMount();
  }

  protected onMount() {}
}

class AsyncComponent extends Component {
  protected onMount() {
    if (this.state === "mounted") { // direct access
      this.loadData();
    }
  }
}

Subclasses read state directly. The base class does not proliferate getters. The tradeoff: subclasses can mutate state incorrectly. The developer trusts that subclass authors understand the lifecycle contract.

Runtime Reality: Why Both Modifiers Disappear in Compiled JavaScript

TypeScript's access modifiers exist only during type checking. The compiler strips them during transpilation. The emitted JavaScript contains no enforcement, no runtime checks, and no access restrictions. A private field becomes an ordinary property accessible via bracket notation or reflection.

The TypeScript handbook states this explicitly: "Like other aspects of TypeScript's type system, private and protected are only enforced during type checking." The compiled output looks identical for public, protected, and private fields.

class Secure {
  private secret: string;
  protected internal: string;
  public visible: string;

  constructor() {
    this.secret = "hidden";
    this.internal = "shared";
    this.visible = "open";
  }
}

The TypeScript compiler targeting ES2015 emits:

class Secure {
  constructor() {
    this.secret = "hidden";
    this.internal = "shared";
    this.visible = "open";
  }
}

All three fields appear as regular properties. No visibility enforcement. A consumer can access secret and internal directly:

const instance = new Secure();
console.log(instance.secret); // "hidden" — no runtime error
console.log(instance["secret"]); // "hidden" — bracket notation bypasses TypeScript

The TypeScript compiler rejects these accesses during type checking, but the runtime allows them. This creates a disconnect: code that fails to compile still runs successfully if the type checks are bypassed.

JavaScript's #private syntax (standardized in ES2022) provides runtime enforcement. Fields declared with # are truly private: the JavaScript engine prevents external access:

class Secure {
  #secret = "hidden";

  getSecret() {
    return this.#secret; // ✓ internal access allowed
  }
}

const instance = new Secure();
console.log(instance.#secret); // SyntaxError: Private field '#secret' must be declared

The # syntax creates hard privacy. The engine throws an error at runtime, not just during compilation. TypeScript supports this syntax and treats #private fields as truly inaccessible.

Feature TypeScript private TypeScript protected JavaScript #private
Compile-time enforcement Yes (TypeScript only) Yes (TypeScript only) Yes (TypeScript only)
Runtime enforcement No No Yes (JavaScript engine)
Subclass access Blocked Allowed Blocked
External access via bracket notation Allowed at runtime Allowed at runtime Blocked
Transpilation to ES5 Becomes public property Becomes public property Polyfilled with WeakMap

Comparison diagram showing TypeScript private versus JavaScript private fields

Teams that need runtime privacy use #private fields. Teams that need inheritance-friendly visibility use protected. Teams that want compile-time guardrails without runtime overhead stick with TypeScript's private and accept the soft enforcement.

The practical implication: access modifiers are documentation for the type checker and other developers. They communicate intent (this field should not leak outside the class), but they do not prevent malicious or careless access at runtime. Security-critical code requires additional runtime validation.

When to Reach for protected vs private: Decision Framework for 2026

The choice between protected and private depends on whether subclasses need field access. The decision tree starts with one question: will any subclass need to read or write this field directly?

If no subclass needs access, use private. This signals that the field is an implementation detail of the declaring class. Subclasses should not depend on it. Future refactors can change the field's type, name, or behavior without breaking subclasses:

class HttpClient {
  private retryCount: number = 0;
  private maxRetries: number = 3;

  async request(url: string): Promise<Response> {
    while (this.retryCount < this.maxRetries) {
      try {
        return await fetch(url);
      } catch (error) {
        this.retryCount++;
      }
    }
    throw new Error("Max retries exceeded");
  }
}

The retryCount and maxRetries fields manage retry logic internal to HttpClient. No subclass needs to know about them. Marking them private allows the developer to replace the retry mechanism (switching to exponential backoff, for example) without touching subclass code.

If subclasses need access, use protected. This signals that the field participates in the inheritance contract. Subclasses can read and write it to implement specialized behavior:

class Repository {
  protected cache: Map<string, unknown> = new Map();

  get(key: string): unknown | undefined {
    return this.cache.get(key);
  }

  set(key: string, value: unknown): void {
    this.cache.set(key, value);
  }
}

class TTLRepository extends Repository {
  private expirations: Map<string, number> = new Map();

  set(key: string, value: unknown, ttl: number): void {
    this.cache.set(key, value); // ✓ direct cache access
    this.expirations.set(key, Date.now() + ttl);
  }

  get(key: string): unknown | undefined {
    const expiration = this.expirations.get(key);
    if (expiration && Date.now() > expiration) {
      this.cache.delete(key); // ✓ direct cache access
      this.expirations.delete(key);
      return undefined;
    }
    return this.cache.get(key);
  }
}

The protected cache allows TTLRepository to implement expiration logic without duplicating the storage mechanism. The base class trusts subclasses to maintain cache consistency.

Scenario Use private Use protected
Field is pure implementation detail ✓
Subclasses will never need access ✓
Field participates in overridable behavior ✓
Subclasses need direct read/write access ✓
Future subclasses are unknown but likely ✓
Field type may change in future versions ✓

Decision flowchart for choosing between protected and private

A common pattern: use private for fields that drive internal algorithms, and protected for fields that represent shared state. If the field's value affects how subclasses implement their behavior, make it protected. If the field exists only to support the base class's methods, make it private.

The exception: library code intended for public consumption. Public APIs often expose hooks (like React component lifecycle methods) but keep all state private. This prevents consumers from accidentally breaking the library's invariants. The library provides protected methods for subclass customization, but keeps data fields locked.

Migration Patterns: Fixing Mid-Refactor Visibility Violations Without Breaking Everything

Teams discover visibility violations mid-refactor when a subclass suddenly cannot access a field that was previously visible. The fix depends on whether the field should have been protected from the start, or whether the subclass access pattern was a mistake.

The first migration: promoting private to protected. This happens when a developer correctly identified shared state but chose the wrong modifier. The fix is mechanical: change private to protected in the base class. TypeScript recompiles without errors. Subclasses gain access:

// Before: private blocks subclass access
class EventEmitter {
  private listeners: Map<string, Function[]> = new Map();

  on(event: string, handler: Function) {
    const handlers = this.listeners.get(event) || [];
    handlers.push(handler);
    this.listeners.set(event, handlers);
  }
}

class LoggingEmitter extends EventEmitter {
  on(event: string, handler: Function) {
    console.log(`Registering ${event}`);
    // Need to access this.listeners but it's private
  }
}

// After: protected allows subclass access
class EventEmitter {
  protected listeners: Map<string, Function[]> = new Map();

  on(event: string, handler: Function) {
    const handlers = this.listeners.get(event) || [];
    handlers.push(handler);
    this.listeners.set(event, handlers);
  }
}

class LoggingEmitter extends EventEmitter {
  on(event: string, handler: Function) {
    console.log(`Registering ${event}`);
    const handlers = this.listeners.get(event) || []; // ✓ now allowed
    handlers.push(handler);
    this.listeners.set(event, handlers);
    super.on(event, handler);
  }
}

The migration preserves the external API. Code that uses EventEmitter continues working. Only subclass implementations change.

The second migration: demoting protected to private with an accessor layer. This happens when subclass access was a mistake. The base class wants to change the field's implementation without breaking subclasses. The fix: add a protected getter/setter and mark the field private:

// Before: protected exposes implementation detail
class Cache {
  protected storage: Map<string, unknown> = new Map();

  get(key: string): unknown {
    return this.storage.get(key);
  }
}

class MetricsCache extends Cache {
  get(key: string): unknown {
    const value = this.storage.get(key); // direct access
    this.recordHit();
    return value;
  }
}

// After: private field with protected accessor
class Cache {
  private storage: Map<string, unknown> = new Map();

  protected getFromStorage(key: string): unknown {
    return this.storage.get(key);
  }

  get(key: string): unknown {
    return this.getFromStorage(key);
  }
}

class MetricsCache extends Cache {
  get(key: string): unknown {
    const value = this.getFromStorage(key); // accessor method
    this.recordHit();
    return value;
  }
}

The base class can now replace storage (switching from Map to WeakMap, for example) without breaking subclasses. The protected accessor method abstracts the storage mechanism.

Migration flowchart for fixing visibility violations

The third migration: extracting a new base class when visibility boundaries conflict. This happens when multiple subclasses need different access to the same field. The fix: create an intermediate base class with looser visibility, and derive restrictive subclasses from it:

// Problem: some subclasses need access, others don't
class Service {
  private connection: DatabaseConnection; // too restrictive
}

class AuditService extends Service {
  // Needs connection access but can't get it
}

class ReadOnlyService extends Service {
  // Doesn't need connection access
}

// Solution: intermediate base class with protected access
abstract class ConnectedService {
  protected connection: DatabaseConnection;

  constructor(conn: DatabaseConnection) {
    this.connection = conn;
  }
}

class AuditService extends ConnectedService {
  async log(event: string): Promise<void> {
    await this.connection.execute("INSERT INTO audit ..."); // ✓ allowed
  }
}

class ReadOnlyService extends ConnectedService {
  // Can access connection but chooses not to
}

The intermediate class ConnectedService exposes the connection to its subclasses. Subclasses that need direct access derive from it. Subclasses that do not derive from a wrapper that hides it.

The key: migrate incrementally. Change one modifier at a time. Run the type checker after each change. Avoid bulk find-and-replace operations that change visibility across dozens of classes simultaneously. Each modifier change is a contract change. Subclasses may depend on the existing contract in subtle ways.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a subclass override a private field from the base class?

No, subclasses cannot access private fields at all. TypeScript treats private as a strict boundary: only the declaring class can read or write the field. A subclass that declares a field with the same name creates a separate, unrelated field. The base class field remains hidden and inaccessible.

Does protected allow access from outside the inheritance chain?

No, protected members are visible only within the class and its subclasses. External code (code that does not extend the class) cannot access protected members. The visibility is strictly limited to the inheritance hierarchy, not to arbitrary code that imports the class.

Why does TypeScript reject assignment between structurally identical classes with private fields?

TypeScript uses nominal typing for private and protected members. Two classes with private fields of the same type and name are incompatible unless they share the same inheritance chain. This prevents accidental mixing of unrelated types that happen to have structurally similar private state.

Can I use protected in an interface?

No, TypeScript interfaces cannot declare protected members. Interfaces define public contracts for objects. Access modifiers like protected and private apply only to class declarations. If you need a contract that includes protected members, use an abstract class instead of an interface.

What happens to protected fields when compiling to JavaScript?

TypeScript strips all access modifiers during transpilation. A protected field becomes a regular public property in the emitted JavaScript. The runtime offers no enforcement. Any code can access the field using direct property access or bracket notation, regardless of the original TypeScript visibility.

Conclusion: Choosing the Right Access Modifier Before Your Team Hits the Wall

The difference between protected and private determines whether subclasses can access base class state. Choosing private locks the field to the declaring class. Choosing protected exposes it to the inheritance chain. Teams that understand this distinction before refactoring avoid mid-build visibility violations and the forced choice between leaky abstractions and redesigned hierarchies. The decision starts with one question: will subclasses need this field? The answer dictates the modifier.
