articles.body_html:
At the end of October, Google opened a plugin catalog for Antigravity, its new platform for agentic development. We built a Publora plugin, submitted it and are now waiting to hear back.

I don't write the code myself. Claude does that, while I ask questions, test things and deal with the submissions. I've become fairly familiar with the last part over the past year.

Chrome rejected our extension twice. Canva took forty-seven days and five versions. Zapier sent us through eight rounds. By now, when I hear "plugin marketplace," I expect documentation, several forms, a reviewer and at least one email explaining what we've done wrong.

Antigravity asked us to fill out a Google Form.

No sign-in, no plugin field, no timeline

It's called the "Antigravity Plugin Interest Form." You don't even need to sign in to Google to submit it.

There's no dedicated field for the plugin repository, so we put our GitHub link in the Documentation URL field. There's nowhere to provide a test account either. Google's documentation calls the catalog "curated," but I couldn't find any published review criteria or expected turnaround time.

We submitted the form and got a confirmation that it had been received. Nothing else so far.

The catalog is only a couple of weeks old, so I don't know whether this is the entire review process or just the first step. The documentation is there, although I still have questions about how some of it works. I'll write about that once we've had a chance to test more.

For now, here's what we submitted and what I managed to check.

What we actually submitted

The plugin is small: two JSON files, nine skills and a logo. The MCP server configuration is one line:

{ "serverUrl": "https://mcp.publora.com/mcp" }

There's no client ID or API key in the configuration. Antigravity uses dynamic client registration with our server, so users don't have to copy a key into the plugin.

The rest is mostly instructions. plugin.json contains three starter prompts, including "show my connected accounts" and "write a LinkedIn post about the latest change in this repo and save it as a draft."

The nine skills contain platform-specific rules and limits.

The gotchas you can already see

The first thing worth checking is OAuth discovery. The address declared in /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource has to match the MCP server address exactly. Antigravity checks this.

We also tested dynamic client registration with Antigravity's callback URL. The server returned 201 for registration, followed by a 302 redirect to the Publora sign-in page.

There were a few smaller surprises.

On the data-collection consent screen, the checkbox is selected by default. Pressing Space clears it, but pressing Enter selects it again. I found this out by trying to get past that screen.

The installer prints ERROR: logging before google.Init during startup. Despite the word ERROR, this wasn't a failure in our tests. The installation continued normally.

And when running agy in the VS Code terminal, part of the interface was invisible, including button labels. The same interface displayed correctly in the regular macOS Terminal. I spent some time looking for buttons that were technically there.

What I checked by hand

I ran agy plugin validate --strict. It passed without errors and detected all nine skills and the MCP server.

Installation worked both from a local folder and directly from GitHub. OAuth completed successfully, and Antigravity reported "signed in to mcp.publora.com."

I called list_connections and got the connected social accounts. I also checked the Bluesky skill: it loaded and correctly identified the 300-character limit.

Then I created a Mastodon draft and deleted it.

That's as far as I tested the publishing workflow. I didn't publish a live post or schedule one, so I can't say those operations work yet. I also tested the CLI, not the graphical Antigravity IDE.

I'll test the rest separately. I'd rather find the problems myself than have the first person who installs it discover them for me.

Google seems to be moving in before it's built

While testing, I noticed something else.

I tried signing in to Gemini CLI with a regular Google account and got this message: "this client is no longer supported… migrate to the Antigravity suite."

At the same time, the Gemini CLI catalog hadn't been updated since mid-October, and our extension never appeared there.

I don't know what Google's longer-term plans are for the two products. But from the outside, it's a strange moment: the new catalog is accepting submissions through a basic form, while at least one sign-in path for the older tool is already pointing users toward Antigravity.

We'd spent time trying to get into the Gemini CLI catalog. Now we're applying to another one, also run by Google. I hope we picked the right door this time.

Where we are now

The plugin is public on GitHub: publora-team/antigravity-publora, under the MIT license. We've submitted the form and are waiting.

There's no published review timeline that I could find, and we haven't been approved yet.

I checked the marketplace announcement and a catalog cache from November 16, which contained more than eighty plugins. I didn't find any social media schedulers. That might mean there's room for Publora, although it tells us nothing about whether Google will accept it.

If we're approved, I'll write a proper setup guide and add Antigravity to our documentation. For now, the plugin is available on GitHub for anyone who wants to try it.

After Chrome, Canva and Zapier, I was prepared for another long review. Instead, I've submitted a Google Form and have no idea when someone will look at it.

I keep checking my email anyway.

Have you submitted anything to the Antigravity catalog yet? Did anyone get back to you, and how long did it take?

articles.title: The Manager Who Doesn't Use AI Has Already Lost: Soft Skills
articles.description: AI writes your minutes, rehearses your difficult conversations, and spots burnout before you do. How...
articles.body_html:
AI writes your minutes, rehearses your difficult conversations, and spots burnout before you do. How about you?

TL;DR: AI removes a manager's cognitive limit. Use it for meetings, feedback, and hard conversations.

This is the second part of the extended article version of my ninth talk at Nerdearla, in September 2026.

The first part covers the hard skills: managing the work.

The talk is in Spanish with English subtitles available.

Nerdbuster and Nerdflix

A quick recap, in case you skipped the first part.

Your job was to maintain Nerdbuster, a video rental system, in production in the 1990s.

Today, you maintain Nerdflix, a streaming platform for nerds, in production.

But one thing never changed:

A manager can't be everywhere at the same time.

Here's the thesis:

What happens when that cognitive limitation disappears?

How to Read This Article

Each section compares Nerdbuster and Nerdflix and uses these markers:

  • 🧩 A skill you can build for your AI assistant
  • 🧭 Human in the loop: the decision that stays with a person
  • ⚠️ A warning: consent, bias, law, or governance

Part 2: Managing People

Everything in the first part was technical.

Now comes the part they didn't teach me at computer science university.

This is outside my comfort zone.

I studied exact sciences, where the most emotional moment is a rounding error. I'm not the person with the best soft skills in the industry.

I had to build them as I became a manager.

AI matters even more nowadays for soft skills.

You move from managing the work to managing people.

Meetings

In Nerdbuster, meetings were crowded and informal.

No action items.

Chronic meeting-itis.

  • "I need you to talk to my customer."
  • "But I'm on another project."
  • "Come anyway."

There are plenty of memes about getting nothing done because you spend the whole day in meetings.

Someone wrote the minutes by hand. Nobody read them.

The minutes said: "Let's do this, and we'll see how."

In Nerdflix, only the relevant people must show up.

You check each attendee's career profile to confirm they can make the decision.

/meeting-profiles: decides who needs to attend. 🧩

The AI and the company brain support them.

You record and transcribe the meeting.

The transcript isn't literal.

With a template, you keep only what matters.

If you spend five minutes talking about football, the minutes skip it.

The AI writes down the minutes and the action items: who said what, what to do, and how you track it.

An architecture decision becomes an architecture decision record (ADR) directly.

/meeting-minutes: writes the transcript, the minutes, and the action items. 🧩

Scheduling happens automatically.

/find-timeslot: books the meeting automatically. 🧩

⚠️ Consent: You tell people when you record them.

🧭 Human in the loop: A person reviews the minutes before publishing them. Otherwise, someone could say "the AI wrote that action item". No. You did.

Managing Up and Stakeholders

In Nerdbuster, managing up meant guessing.

You guessed what your boss wanted to hear, and you showed up with the answer before they asked the question.

The result was a long, detailed report and a weekend lost to bureaucracy.

In Nerdflix, the AI translates the technical status into business impact.

One page. No jargon.

/executive-summary: fits the status on one page. 🧩

The AI is your sparring partner.

You use it in adversarial mode: "I have to say this, and a business person will sit in front of me."

The AI tells you if your tone and language fit that audience.

You can ask it to play an aggressive customer who pressures you commercially.

You train with AI sparring, and you walk in with your answers ready.

(I wish I had this when I started managing).

Managing up is no longer guessing.

It's communicating well and fast, in the language of the person who decides.

/translate-to-business-language: turns technical status into business impact. 🧩

🧭 Human in the loop: Reviewing your commitments is critical. The AI can't promise on your behalf.

Communications, Auto-Replies, and Alerts

In Nerdbuster, you wrote to a customer on long email.

You copied half the company, just in case.

The longer it was, the more serious it looked.

Email chains grew out of control. "RE: RE: RE:" until you lost count.

Photo by Antoni Shkraba from Pexels

Nobody tracked them, and nobody knew who should answer.

At some point, the thread faded away. Until someone brought it back.

There were no clear action items, but plenty of people in copy, each one hoarding the thread.

In Nerdflix, you write much shorter messages. Straight to the point.

/summarize-status: summarizes where each thread stands. 🧩

And there's something new: you don't know if a person or an AI agent reads your message on the other side.

You write differently, knowing that.

/adversarial-customer-role: plays a tough customer so you test your message before you send it. 🧩

The AI is your friend and also your foe.

😈 Inbox zero.

Your inbox isn't a to-do list.

You process everything that comes in:
-with a rule
-with the company brain
-with your attention-
-with an AI agent.

You work with empty backlogs.

The AI summarizes and prioritizes the threads and the alerts, and drafts the replies.

For routine messages, you can use an agent like OpenClaw or Hermes.

/triage-inbox: sorts and prioritizes your inbox. 🧩

🧭 Human in the loop: Every message carries your signature and your tone, not the plastic AI tone.

⚠️ Governance: Turning on auto-replies and reading confidential information is never your decision alone. It needs explicit approval from your organization governance and the least privilege possible. That makes it a governance decision. These agents aren't approved products in most companies. You should never upload confidential data to an AI your company hasn't approved. It can leak.

🧭 Human in the loop: The manager decides what gets automated and what doesn't.

Delegating

In Nerdbuster, delegating meant handing out tickets at the planning meeting.

You assigned them to whoever was available.

Or to whoever had fewer sticky notes on the whiteboard.

People were treated as interchangeable, fungible resources.

"I had a programmer. Another programmer arrived. Same thing."

You know people aren't the same and you should treat them kindly and individually. You should ban the word resource from your Taylorist language.

In Nerdflix, delegating well is something else.

You shouldn't say "you have to do this task".

You say: "This is for a critical customer. It goes to production in a week. We're late. Something else comes after it."

You explain the why to the AI. You explain it to people too.

You drop the Taylorist "do this as requested, never mind why".

Context empowers people. With enough autonomy, they take responsibility.

The context comes from the company brain.

/delegate-with-context: pulls the context from the company brain and structures the delegation. 🧩

The team takes ownership, with autonomy.

Open your AI model and type:

I need to organize the next Nerdflix sprint.

That's a mediocre prompt.

It's vague. It has no context and no constraints. It hands the whole decision over to the AI.

Now try something different:

ROLE: Act as the Engineering Manager of an 8-person team on Nerdflix.

CONTEXT:
We have 12 pending tickets.
Three of them impact customers.
Two of them block other work.
We have an external dependency that will probably arrive late.
The team is showing signs of burnout.
The project deadline can't move.

TASK: Help me decide what should go into the next sprint.

CONSTRAINT: Don't make the decision for me.
First, identify the relevant variables.
Then propose three different strategies.

OUTPUT: For each strategy, explain:
- What we gain
- What we sacrifice
- What risk we introduce
- What additional information we would need

Finally, challenge my decision.
Act as a manager who disagrees with me.

You didn't ask it to write a sprint.

You asked it to help you think.

That difference is huge.

If you don't want to build a skill, you should at least write structured prompts.

You don't carry that context in your head.

It comes from the company brain: the accumulated memory of decisions, post-mortems, and incidents.

It doesn't appear by magic. You build it, session after session.

The better you build it, the better you delegate, because you give both the AI and the human the why and not just the what.

🧭 Human in the loop: The manager decides what goes into the sprint.

Post-Mortems

In Nerdbuster, the post-mortem was a tense meeting.

Everybody looked for a scapegoat. 🐐 The winner was usually whoever missed the meeting.


Photo by Yan Krukau from Pexels

The informal notes got lost. Nobody left with clear action items.

That was a culture of fear.

In Nerdflix, the post-mortem is blameless.

You learn from the process and improve it.

The AI transcribes the ceremony and extracts concrete action items.

You cut any blaming live.

The action items belong to the team, not to people.

If a person needs to adjust something, you handle it in private, with journaling.

Good and bad cases feed the company brain.

/post-mortem-minutes: transcribes the ceremony and extracts the action items. 🧩

🧭 Human in the loop: The facilitator cuts the blaming and rephrases it in generic terms, so nothing points at a person. A person reviews each case before it goes into the company brain.

Ceremonies: Stand-Ups, Retros, and Other Rituals

In Nerdbuster, the stand-up was literally standing up for thirty minutes.

It ended up as a status and time report.

Someone spent ten minutes explaining they had met with another team the day before. Everybody else was bored.

The retrospective was a wall of generic sticky notes: "what went well, what went wrong", with no real actions.

Photo by Mikhail Nilov from Pexels

In Nerdflix, the stand-up meeting is async.

Everybody writes. The AI builds the summary and flags real blockers.

You don't care what each person is doing.

You care about what's blocking them.

/standup-summary: summarizes the async stand-up and flags blockers. 🧩

Unblocking people is your job. Honestly, it's your only job.

A bit of informal chat is fine. You're human.

But if an update brings no action item and no blocker, nobody needs to hear it.

The AI also finds patterns across retrospectives.

It tells you, anonymously: "The last six meeting minutes mention that another team doesn't collaborate."

You don't need to ask. It detects the pattern. That's the agentic side of AI.

If a complaint repeats three times, it's a pattern, and you write it down so it never repeats again.

/retro-patterns: groups repeated complaints across sprints, not just the last one. 🧩

🧭 Human in the loop: The AI groups. The team decides what action to take.

The Talent Journey

In Nerdbuster, teams were rigid.

Job requisitions came with fixed profiles, based on effort estimations.

"We need a junior Java programmer." That was all you knew.

You interviewed with a written exam and an algorithm on the whiteboard. That tested memory, not judgment.

Dynamic programming questions that nobody, the interviewer included, ever used on the job.

Onboarding meant two months of theory before touching the code.

"Read these courses, mark them done, fill in the forms. Then we'll see."

Offboarding was an HR formality: a form, an email, and the knowledge walking out the door.

In Nerdflix, it's a single journey.

Teams are flexible and built around talent and timing.

You find which skills are missing and look for those profiles inside or outside the company.

You interview with a fluent conversation and an ambiguous scenario.

You tell the candidate up front: "You'll be recorded. The AI and I will evaluate you."

The AI takes the notes and evaluates tone and English proficiency.

The candidate uses AI for the technical part. You evaluate their judgment and how they supervise the AI.

/match-positions-to-skills: builds flexible teams based on talent. 🧩

New people are productive from day one.

The senior keeps the judgment calls.

When someone leaves, you audit agents, skills, and the company brain, not just the laptop.

/code-review, /spec-review, /process-evaluation: make new people productive from day one. 🧩

You also guide the newcomer with a flexible journey:

/junior-mentor: supports juniors while the senior keeps the judgment calls. 🧩

Letting someone go is also part of the journey:

/offboarding-audit: revokes access to agents, skills, and the company brain. 🧩

⚠️ Bias: You supervise the AI for bias in every hiring step.

⚠️ Law: You get advice on your local labor laws.

🧭 Human in the loop: The team decides who gets hired, not a score. Onboarding includes mentoring and review.

Team Health and Individual Feedback

In Nerdbuster, you detected overload when deliveries were already failing. Too late.

Burnout management was reactive and based on gut feeling.

Feedback happened once a year, in a performance review tied to the bonus.

You used the feedback sandwich 🥪 and other recipes.

In Nerdflix, aggregated team patterns, like working hours and commits, suggest a conversation.

Never the detail of a single person.

The AI warns you: "Commits are consistently happening outside working hours."

You don't surveil anyone. You spot a burnout pattern.

You also read patterns in the ceremonies and in one-on-ones with AI transcripts.

Feedback is constant, in small doses.

The AI captures situational notes, so you avoid recency bias in the performance review.

/one-on-ones: prepares and records your one-on-ones. 🧩

A review that looks only at the last month is always unfair.

With notes, you can say: "In March, this didn't go well. Two months later, I saw you learned it."

It shows people that you pay attention.

You take the notes when things happen. Looking back, the traces are hard to find.

/journaling: takes notes in every meeting. 🧩

⚠️ Team signal, not individual surveillance: You look at team patterns, never at one person's activity.

⚠️ Consent: Transcribing or recording always requires consent.

🧭 Human in the loop: The manager gives the feedback. The AI detects signals. It doesn't diagnose people.

AI as a Sparring Partner for Difficult Conversations

In Nerdbuster, you rehearsed for five minutes in the hallway, or you just walked in.

You imagined the other person's reaction by projecting your own logic.

The difficult conversation was a Taylorist asymmetry: you informed, you didn't talk.

In Nerdflix, you practice with the AI in two directions.

First, the AI plays the difficult counterpart, so you rehearse your answers before the real conversation. It shows you where the person may get defensive.

Then, "Act as...": the AI becomes that person, so you understand their logic before you talk to them.

Regular one-on-ones use open questions, always practiced with the AI first.

You lean on the AI to think before you act.

Like this talk, actually.

🧭 Human in the loop: What to say and how to act is the person's decision.

Professional Development: Evaluate, Correct, Plan

In Nerdbuster, the evaluation was a generic form, unrelated to the actual role.

The improvement plan was an HR formality, the last step before firing someone, with no follow-up.

The career plan was arbitrary. Seniority or performance?

In Nerdflix, it's a single flow.

You evaluate against a competency specification by role and seniority, with evidence: pull requests, incidents, design decisions, and one-on-one notes.

"You're here. The next step needs you there. This is the gap."

/compare-competencies: compares the evidence against the role specification. 🧩

You don't talk in abstract terms like "work on your autonomy".

You point to the specific case where autonomy was missing.

The process improvement plan comes directly from the review gap. It's real support.

The career plan maps possible transitions against the missing competencies.

/weekly-check-ins: follows the improvement plan week by week. 🧩

Promotions are also part of the people journey:

/promotion-gap: maps career transitions against the missing competencies. 🧩

🧭 Human in the loop: The manager runs the evaluation and the conversation. Extending, closing, or ending an improvement plan is decided together with Talent. The manager builds the career plan together with the person.

Salaries

In Nerdbuster, salaries were an arbitrary one-on-one negotiation.

How much you asked. How much the company dared to offer. How well you negotiated.

No market data.

Hallway gossip about who earns what was the closest thing to a salary survey.

Salary inequity, naturally.

In Nerdflix, you look at the sysarmy salary survey.

You compare the profile against a real market sample.

You calibrate. You don't guess.

/calibrate-role: calibrates the salary band for the role. 🧩

You do it all the time, because the market moves.

You might learn someone is unhappy this month because the market pays more.

/salary-benchmark: compares the profile against the market. 🧩

🧭 Human in the loop: The company makes the final call on the salary band, with the manager's calibration.

Other People Topics

I left out other big topics on the people side:

  • AI usage governance
  • Remote team rituals and culture
  • Diversity and inclusion
  • Peer conflicts
  • Wellness
  • Peer mentoring and coaching
  • Budget and contractor or vendor management

Please write new topic ideas for a third article in the comments.

The Manager's Territory

Managers added value by coordinating people.

With five, ten, or twenty people, the problem was always the same: you couldn't be everywhere.

Meetings, reports, dashboards, and objectives and key results (OKRs) all solved the same problem.

The real limitation was always the manager's cognitive capacity.

Now there's a machine that reads, summarizes, compares, and challenges decisions.

That goes beyond automating administrative tasks.

It's entering the manager's territory.

Human judgment is the most important thing.

That's why they hire you.

The AI doesn't have human judgment.

For now.

Automate, Operate, Augment

There are three levels of AI use:

  1. Automate: the AI does a task on its own.
  2. Operate: the AI runs a workflow or a sequence of tasks.
  3. Augment: the AI dramatically improves your ability to decide.

Image by boundsmarnie from Pixabay

This article is mostly about the third level.

That level separates the chatbot that summarizes your email from the AI that challenges your management decisions.

You shouldn't stay at the first or second level. You need to be augmented.

People ask me where to download my skills.

You can't. You build your own. They're personal.

You start by asking the AI: "Create a skill for me." Then you use it, refine it, and let it mature.

You build all these 🧩 skills by interacting with the AI, and you script the repeatable steps.

You can take these three concepts back to work.

Nobody Taught You

Managers aren't early adopters.

But you're as replaceable as any other role.

I didn't show you any specific tool.

This isn't theory. You can apply it right now.

I'd rather leave you with the itch.

You keep hearing that "AI won't replace you".

That's true.

But a manager who uses it well will.

It's not your fault. Nobody taught you.

Not your university, not your company, not YouTube.

Today, that changes.

articles.title: The 'Free' remove.bg Replacement Costs $144 a Year. Do the Maths First.
articles.description: Three days ago I wrote that remove.bg dies on December 1, and that the free tool on your own machine...
articles.body_html:
Three days ago I wrote that remove.bg dies on December 1, and that the free tool on your own machine could replace it. The piece did well. Then deanlee left a comment I have been thinking about ever since. He asked the question I had dodged in the original piece: at what point does paying for Canva actually cost less than paying per removal somewhere else?

I dodged it with a soft sentence. Something about the subscription maybe being the saner choice for heavy users. That is not an answer. It is a shrug dressed up as advice. So I spent this morning doing the sums properly, re-weighing the files from that first test, and recounting the pixels behind a number I now regret printing. Here is the honest version.

Problem 1: the subscription costs $144 a year, and the break-even is 12 removals a month

Canva Pro is $18 a month if you pay monthly, or $144 a year if you pay once. That works out to $12 a month. One person only. Those are the US prices, read from Canva's own pricing page in October 2026 — Canva charges different amounts in other countries, so if your pricing page shows a different currency, run the same sums with your own numbers. The background remover sits inside that paid plan, and the free plan does not have it.

Now the other side. After December 1, the thing you compare it against is not remove.bg's $9 subscription. That plan stops existing. The honest comparison is paying per image, and remove.bg's smallest one-off pack is $3 for 3 credits. One credit takes the background out of one photo. That is $1 a removal.

Twelve dollars divided by one dollar is twelve. If you pay Canva yearly, you need to remove 12 backgrounds a month before the subscription beats paying a dollar a time. Pay monthly instead, and the line moves to 18 a month.

Bigger packs bend the number. The $49 pack works out to 65 cents a removal, and against that Canva only wins past 19 removals a month on yearly billing, 28 on monthly. The $199 pack drops it to 40 cents, and then you need 30 a month yearly, 45 monthly. So the real answer is a range, not a single number: somewhere between 12 and 30 a month, depending on how you buy the one-off credits.

And one more honest wrinkle. If you already pay for Canva because you use its templates or its brand tools, the remover costs you nothing extra. Your break-even is zero. This maths only bites if background removal is the thing pushing you to pay in the first place.

One gap I could not close: several reviews this year say Canva's paid AI tools share a monthly allowance, and I could not confirm whether the background remover draws from it. If you cut out hundreds of photos a month, look at the limit on your own plan before you assume it is bottomless.

Problem 2: the cheap price you remember is a ghost

This is the part that changes the answer most. In my first piece I quoted remove.bg's $9 plan, 40 images, about 23 cents each. That number is real, and it is also dead in two weeks. Subscriptions end on December 1 and unused one-off credits expire the same day. Comparing Canva against 23 cents is comparing against a price nobody will be able to pay after the shutdown.

The fair comparison is what you can actually buy on December 2: a dollar a removal at the small end. That is the number the break-even above uses.

If you still hold remove.bg credits, use them before December 1. After that they are gone, and so is the argument that paid removal costs 23 cents.

Problem 3: the PNG weighs more than I told you

In the first piece I said the shoe went in as a 128 KB JPEG and came out as a 632 KB PNG, and I waved at compression as the fix. I should have weighed it properly then. I have now, using the same cut-outs from that morning.

Same shoe, same pixels, three formats. The PNG is 632 KB. Saved as WebP with the transparency kept, at a quality setting where I could not spot a difference at normal viewing size, it is 94 KB. That is 6.75 times smaller. Flattened onto white and saved as a JPEG, it is 99 KB, or 6.37 times smaller. The portrait is worse: a 1.56 MB PNG becomes a 192 KB WebP, 8.13 times smaller, or a 234 KB JPEG, 6.69 times smaller.

So the "five times" figure floating around my draft notes was wrong in the generous direction. It is six to eight times on real photos with a real subject. The one exception was the mountain lake photo, where the PNG was only 3.5 times the WebP, because there was almost nothing in the file to compress in the first place.

I also built a small test page with one shoe on it, in all three formats, and measured what actually travels down the wire. The PNG page moves 632 KB. The WebP page moves 94 KB. Scale that to a shop with 40 product shots and the PNG version ships 24.7 MB of images where the WebP version ships 3.7 MB. That is the difference between a page that opens and a page your customer stares at.

The fix costs nothing. Convert the cut-out to WebP before it goes on a page, and keep the PNG only as your master copy. Lossless WebP barely helps, about 1.4 times smaller, so it has to be the lossy setting to matter.

Problem 4: the 71.7% number was right, and it meant nothing

This is the one I owe readers a correction on. In the first piece I printed "71.7% transparent" for the mountain lake photo, then said in the next paragraph that the number meant nothing because the remaining 28% was a grey blob. Both halves were true, and printing the number at all was still a mistake, because a table makes any number look measured.

I recounted it pixel by pixel from the actual file. 689,221 of 961,200 pixels are fully transparent. That is 71.70%. The number was correct. The shoe was 73.48% against the 73.5% I printed, and the portrait 66.78% against 66.8%. All three check out.

But here is what the recount found that the table hid. In the lake photo, only 7 pixels in the entire image are fully solid. Seven. The other 28.3% of the picture is made of half-transparent pixels, a thin wash of grey where the tool could not decide what was subject and what was sky. A transparency percentage counts pixels. It cannot tell you whether the pixels it kept form a shoe or a smudge. No percentage can. Only looking at the picture can, and when I looked, the picture was a ghost.

The recount also explains the file sizes above. Even the good cut-outs are mostly half-transparent edge pixels, 24% of the shoe and 32% of the portrait. Soft edges are why the tool looks good, and soft edges are exactly what makes a PNG balloon.

What I would actually do

If you remove backgrounds a few times a month, do not buy a subscription for it. Pay a dollar when you need one, or run the free tool on your own machine and spend eight seconds a photo instead. Twelve removals a month is the line, and most people never cross it.

If you cross it every month, and you do it inside Canva already, pay yearly and stop thinking about it. The $144 works out to $12 a month, and the per-removal price stops mattering.

And whatever you switch to, do not ship the PNG. Convert it. The cut-out is free. The page weight is the bill you pay later, every time someone opens your site.

Now I want the other side of this. How many backgrounds do you actually remove in a month, the real count, not the guess? And if you already switched away from remove.bg, what did you switch to, and what did it cost once you counted everything? If enough of you answer with real numbers, I will run the same maths on your answers and print the correction if I got any of this wrong.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: What Makes a Music Box Go 'Tink' (and How to Fake It in Web Audio)
articles.description: What Makes a Music Box Go 'Tink' (and How to Fake It in Web Audio)   A music box is a simple...
articles.body_html:
What Makes a Music Box Go 'Tink' (and How to Fake It in Web Audio)

A music box is a simple machine. A brass cylinder with pins spins against a steel comb. The teeth are cut to different lengths, so each one rings at its own pitch and dies out fast. Long teeth sing low, short teeth sing high. The melody is just the arrangement of pins.

I spent a while rebuilding that machine in a browser: an 18-note virtual music box, C5 to F6, the standard movement size for souvenir boxes. The hard part was never the notes. It was the timbre.

The fourth partial is the whole trick

Pluck one tooth on a real box and you hear three things: a bright fundamental, a very strong fourth partial (four times the fundamental frequency), and a fast decay. The fourth partial is what makes it metallic instead of flutey. A plain sine wave sounds like a test tone. Add its fourth partial, let both decay quickly, and it sounds like a music box.

The voice is three oscillators into one gain:

function playTooth(n, when) {
  const ctx = getCtx();
  const t = when === undefined ? ctx.currentTime : when;
  const f = freqs[n];

  const g = ctx.createGain();
  g.gain.setValueAtTime(0.42, t);
  g.gain.exponentialRampToValueAtTime(0.001, t + 1.6);

  // fundamental
  const o1 = ctx.createOscillator();
  o1.type = 'sine'; o1.frequency.value = f;

  // the signature: 4th partial, strong but short-lived
  const o2 = ctx.createOscillator();
  o2.type = 'sine'; o2.frequency.value = f * 4;
  const g2 = ctx.createGain();
  g2.gain.value = 0.4;
  g2.gain.exponentialRampToValueAtTime(0.001, t + 0.9);

  // a faint shimmer one octave above that, gone in 300ms
  const o3 = ctx.createOscillator();
  o3.type = 'sine'; o3.frequency.value = f * 8;
  const g3 = ctx.createGain();
  g3.gain.value = 0.06;
  g3.gain.exponentialRampToValueAtTime(0.001, t + 0.3);

  // steel comb has no low-end mud
  const hp = ctx.createBiquadFilter();
  hp.type = 'highpass'; hp.frequency.value = 300;

  o1.connect(g); o2.connect(g2); g2.connect(g);
  o3.connect(g3); g3.connect(g);
  g.connect(hp); hp.connect(ctx.destination);

  o1.start(t); o2.start(t); o3.start(t);
  o1.stop(t + 1.7); o2.stop(t + 1.0); o3.stop(t + 0.4);
}

The decay envelope does most of the work. The fundamental hangs around for 1.7 seconds; the fourth partial is gone in under one. That gap is the "tink" followed by a fading body. The 300 Hz highpass keeps it from sounding like a soft pad. Music boxes are bright. There's no warmth to protect.

Eighteen teeth, eighteen frequencies:

const teeth = ['C5','C#5','D5','D#5','E5','F5','F#5','G5','G#5','A5','A#5','B5','C6','C#6','D6','D#6','E6','F6'];
const freqs = {};
teeth.forEach(n => {
  const m = n.match(/([A-G])(#?)(\d)/);
  const base = {C:0,D:2,E:4,F:5,G:7,A:9,B:11}[m[1]] + (m[2] === '#' ? 1 : 0);
  const oct = parseInt(m[3]);
  freqs[n] = 440 * Math.pow(2, (base - 9) / 12 + oct - 4);
});

Making it look like a music box, not a keyboard

My first version rendered the 18 teeth as vertical bars in a row. It worked, and it was wrong. A comb isn't a keyboard: it's one steel plate with teeth cut into it, hanging over a cylinder. So I redrew it:

  • One metal spine across the top, teeth hanging down from it. Long teeth on the left (C5, 98 px), stepping down to short teeth on the right (F6, 46 px). Graduated length is the whole instrument.
  • A brass pin cylinder under the teeth tips. The pins are pure CSS, a radial-gradient dot pattern on an 11×12 px tile repeated over a rounded gradient bar.
  • A crank on the right, walnut box, red felt, lid propped open. All divs and gradients. No images, no canvas.

The rotation is the fun part. No WebGL. A rotating cylinder is just the pin pattern's background-position scrolling in a loop:

@keyframes mbspin {
  from { background-position: 0 0; }
  to   { background-position: 0 120px; }
}

The dot tile repeats every 12 px, so 120 px is exactly ten revolutions. Seamless loop, for free. When you pluck one tooth, the cylinder takes a quick quarter turn instead (0 to 32 px in 0.38 s). Re-triggering the same CSS animation per note needs the reflow trick: remove the class, force layout with void el.offsetWidth, add it back. The crank spins while the demo plays, 0.85 s per turn.

Recording without a server

Record stores note events as {f, t} pairs, then replays them through the same voice graph into an OfflineAudioContext:

const off = new OfflineAudioContext(1, len, 44100);
recNotes.forEach(rn => {
  const t = rn.t;
  // ...same gain ramps, same three oscillators, same highpass...
  o1.start(t); o2.start(t); o3.start(t);
  o1.stop(t + 1.7); o2.stop(t + 1.0); o3.stop(t + 0.4);
});
off.startRendering().then(buf => {
  const wav = encodeWav(buf);
  const blob = new Blob([wav], { type: 'audio/wav' });
  download.href = URL.createObjectURL(blob);
});

The WAV encoder is about 40 lines: RIFF header, fmt chunk, PCM16 samples. Because the render runs the same oscillator graph, the export sounds exactly like what you heard live. Nothing is uploaded anywhere.

Details that mattered more than expected

Plucking fires on mousedown and touchstart, not click. A music box plucks at the press, not the release, and click adds a delay you can feel in fast runs. preventDefault stops the double fire on touch.

Keyboard support maps one key per tooth in pitch order (A W S E D F T G Y H U J K O L P ; '), same layout as the piano tools on the site, so muscle memory carries over.

AudioContext gets created lazily and resumed on the first gesture. Browsers require a gesture before audio starts, and you don't want a suspended context eating your first pluck.

The demo melody is Brahms' Lullaby. Public domain, and the classic music-box tune since 1868.

Fourteen languages, one comb

The tool ships in 14 languages, including RTL (Arabic) and no-space scripts (Thai, Japanese). UI strings come from a per-language file loaded at runtime. The instrument itself is language neutral. The comb renders with dir="ltr" internally so low-to-high tooth order stays physically correct on RTL pages.

What I'd change next

The voice is a model, not a sample. It's small, it loads instantly, and everyone hears the same sound, which is why I kept it synthesized. A version two would add a slightly inharmonic second partial (real teeth aren't perfect sines) and per-tooth detune so chords beat naturally. A sampled comb through a convolution reverb would be closer again. I don't know that I'd want that tradeoff: a few kilobytes of JavaScript vs a sample library.

Try it: soundtool.tools/virtual-music-box. Click the teeth, hit the demo, record something, download the WAV.

I built this tool. It's part of soundtool.tools, a set of browser-based audio utilities.

articles.title: How I Built Haze: Live WebGL Backgrounds While Learning Shaders
articles.description: So, it's been a while. Almost two years since my last article here, and work has kept me really busy....
articles.body_html:
So, it's been a while. Almost two years since my last article here, and work has kept me really busy. But I'm back, and I've got something to show you :)

Have you ever landed on a website where the background moves? Soft gradients drifting into each other, ribbons of colour, little points of light following your cursor? I've always loved those. And for a long time, I had an idea sitting in my notes app: what if adding one to your site was as easy as adding an image?

Two weeks ago, I finally shipped it. It's called Haze, and it gives you live backgrounds for your website. You pick a design, make it yours in the browser, then paste one tag into your site. It's under 9 KB, with no dependencies.

In this article, I'll walk you through why I built it, why I finally did it now, what I learned about shaders along the way, and what building it with AI was actually like. Let's jump right into it!

Just want to add one to your site? Skip to How to Use It

Where the Idea Came From

I've always been drawn to dynamic landing pages. Microinteractions, things that react when you move your mouse, and generally anything that makes a website feel alive and look different from the rest. If you've read my article on using mousemove to reveal background images, you already know this ;)

The problem is that the really nice ones are usually hard to add. You either pull in a 3D library, drop in a heavy background video, or spend hours writing shader code. That's a lot of work for a hero section.

What I wanted was something plug and play. Something I could drop into my own website or a client's project in a minute, without thinking about WebGL at all.

Why Now?

Honestly, Haze wasn't the only idea in that notes app. I've been collecting them for years, and most are small, design-related things I never found the time to build.

Two things changed this year.

First, I started the shaders section of Bruno Simon's Three.js Journey course. For the first time, the moving backgrounds I loved stopped feeling like magic, and I could see how they're actually made.

Second, AI tools got good enough that I could build an idea in days instead of months. So I figured, why not now? I picked the idea I'd held onto the longest and started there.

So, What is a Shader?

Shaders could sound intimidating, but the idea behind them is simple. Here's how I like to think about it.

Think of your screen as a grid of tiny squares called pixels. A shader is one rule that every pixel follows, all at the same time, to pick its own colour:

Your GPU (your computer's graphics chip) gets millions of pixels to follow that rule at once, about 60 times a second. That's really it!

Haze's backgrounds are just cleverer rules: ones that bend, ripple and blend colours, so you get ribbons, particles and soft gradients instead of a flat fade.

Because the GPU does all the work, the background stays sharp on any screen size, and it weighs a few kilobytes where a background video weighs megabytes. Haze also makes sure it doesn't waste your visitors' battery:

  • It stops drawing when it's scrolled off screen or the tab is hidden.
  • It shows a still frame for people who prefer reduced motion.
  • If a browser doesn't support WebGL, a CSS gradient in the same colours shows instead, so nothing breaks.

How to Use It

Here's the fun part. Go to haze.mitolu.dev, pick one of the 20 designs (ribbons, particles, paper hills, soft gradients and more), and open it in the studio. There, you can change the colours, speed and scale, and pick a cursor effect: stir, trail or pixels.

When you're happy with it, click Export and copy the tag. To use it as the background of a hero section, add the following to your HTML:

<script src="https://haze.mitolu.dev/v1/haze.js" defer></script>

<section class="hero">
  <haze-gradient preset="silk"></haze-gradient>
  <h1>Your headline</h1>
</section>

Then, in your CSS, place the background behind your content:

.hero {
  position: relative;
  isolation: isolate;
  min-height: 100vh;
}

.hero haze-gradient {
  position: absolute;
  inset: 0;
  z-index: -1;
}

And that's it! The script loads once, and <haze-gradient> draws the design wherever you put it. The tag you copy from the studio carries your own colours and settings in place of preset="silk".

If you're working in React or Next.js, you can export it as a React component instead. There's also a vanilla JS option if you'd rather not use a custom element.

Using Haze on WordPress

The easiest way is a Custom HTML block, which lets you paste the whole hero, script included.

  1. Open the page in the block editor.
  2. Click the + button, search for Custom HTML, and add the block where you want the hero.
  3. Paste the following code, and swap the line for the tag you copied from the studio: 
<script src="https://haze.mitolu.dev/v1/haze.js" defer></script>

<section style="position: relative; isolation: isolate; min-height: 80vh; display: grid; place-content: center; text-align: center; color: #fff;">
  <haze-gradient preset="silk" style="position: absolute; inset: 0; z-index: -1;"></haze-gradient>
  <h1>Your headline</h1>
  <p>A short line about what you do.</p>
</section>
  1. Click Preview to see it moving, then publish.

The styles are inline here so you don't have to touch your theme's CSS. If you're on WordPress.com, note that adding scripts needs a plan that allows plugins. Self-hosted WordPress works out of the box.

Using Haze on Framer

In Framer, you'll use an Embed component and place it behind your hero's content.

  1. Select your hero section, and set its position so its children can be pinned (Framer frames do this by default).
  2. Open the Insert menu, find Embed, and drop it inside the hero.
  3. In the Embed's settings, set the type to HTML and paste: 
<script src="https://haze.mitolu.dev/v1/haze.js" defer></script>
<haze-gradient preset="silk"></haze-gradient>
  1. Set the Embed's position to Absolute, pin it to all four edges, and set both width and height to fill the section.
  2. Move the Embed to the bottom of the layers list, so your text sits on top of it.

The <haze-gradient> element fills whatever box it's in, so once the Embed covers the section, the background does too. Preview the site to see it moving, since Framer's canvas doesn't always run embedded scripts while editing.

Two Weeks Later

I posted it on Twitter and LinkedIn, and about 120 people have tried it so far (from site analytics). That's a great start, and I'm grateful for every one of them.

But my favourite part happened in my DMs. Four people reached out because they wanted a background like this on their personal websites. Two of them said seeing my post made them want to pick up building their portfolio again, which honestly made my week.

So I helped themset it up, and each one was on a different platform:

  • a plain HTML website
  • WordPress
  • Framer
  • a Next.js app

It worked on all of them, which was exactly the point. One tag, wherever your site lives. On top of those 120 users, four real people using it on their real websites tells me the idea works.

Conclusion

And there you have it! An idea from my notes app, finally out in the world.

This is just the first version. I'm still exploring more shaders, and Haze is where everything I explore with will go next: WebGPU, textures and more designs. I've also got some more exciting updates coming soon, so stay tuned! And if you've had an idea sitting in your notes app for a while, maybe this is your sign to start!

Haze is live on Product Hunt today! If you'd like to support it, I'd really appreciate an upvote or a comment there. Support Haze on Product Hunt

Try it out at haze.mitolu.dev, and if you put one on your site, please share it with me. I'd love to see it.

If you have a question, kindly leave your feedback in the comments section.

Thanks for reading, and happy coding!

Resources for Further Learning

If this got you curious about shaders, these are the resources that helped me most:

  • An Introduction to Shaders on Frontend Horse
  • The Book of Shaders
  • Three.js Journey by Bruno Simon
  • Shadertoy: thousands of shaders you can run and tweak in the browser. Great for inspiration.
  • Yuri Artiukh's YouTube channel

articles.title: Could I Still Do This From Scratch?
articles.description: The thing that every dev I know is quietly worrying about is not AI taking their job. It's losing the...
articles.body_html:
The thing that every dev I know is quietly worrying about is not AI taking their job. It's losing the skill to do their job.

We're not talking about it out loud because it feels like admitting weakness, and because these tools are genuinely powerful. You can roll out a feature in an afternoon that previously took you a week. Autocomplete guesses what you're thinking. A chat agent lets you restructure that flaky module you've been avoiding for months. But then in that in-between moment, the third or fourth prompt, the third or fourth tab-tab-tab-accept cycle, that quiet question pops up: could I still do this from scratch?

Now don't get me wrong, I'm not saying that devs couldn't write a for loop if they wanted to. I'm saying that this part is what's fading. The deep work of wrestling with a problem, thinking it through, fumbling around in the dark until the solution crystallizes. Because instead of spending fifteen minutes thinking through the problem, the model gives you the answer in fifteen seconds, so what you're doing is no longer building something. You're reviewing it, which is a far less taxing and less creative task.

The research is starting to catch up with this concern. In a Microsoft study presented at CHI 2025, 319 knowledge workers showed a clear trend: the higher the trust in AI-generated content, the lower the level of critical thinking. The change in workflow is not about problem solving, but about checking and integrating. In another study, this time from MIT Media Lab about essay writing, people who used LLMs were the ones with the worst brain connectivity. They called it cognitive debt. Even productivity is more doubtful than the hype says: in a 2025 study by METR, experienced open source developers using AI tools turned out to be slower than those who didn't, but convinced themselves of the opposite.

All the devs I know have felt this, not as some abstract fear, but as a concrete experience of reaching for an answer and realizing the shelf is empty. I don't need a study to tell me that the knowledge I used to have is slipping away. That the syntax I once produced on autopilot is now a few keystrokes and a prompt away. That the kind of instinct only a developer who's been through dozens of bad architectural decisions can have is now being outsourced to a model that has seen a million architectures but never lived inside one.

The scary part is that it happens under the radar. You're still writing good code, because the model writes good code. You're still getting good performance reviews. You're still shipping. Until you're not, and that's when the tools don't work: when a weird bug shows up, when a novel constraint hits, when an edge case the training data never saw appears. Only then do you realize if there's actually a developer under the hood, or if it's just a workflow.

No one wants to go back to the old days of writing boilerplate the hard way. But the devs who are quietly preparing are doing it in the not-so-cool way: writing some code without AI, wrestling through the confusion, keeping those weak muscles working. The scary part is not that AI will replace you. It's that one day you'll wake up and you'll have replaced yourself, one accepted suggestion at a time.

articles.title: Git 2.56's git add --resolved only checks conflict markers while git still calls a file unmerged
articles.description: I tested Git 2.56's new add --resolved flag: it kept an unrelated edit out of a merge commit, but its conflict-marker check stopped working the moment the index stopped calling a file unmerged.
articles.body_html:
Git 2.56 shipped a new flag for the oldest bad habit in merge conflict resolution: typing git add . the moment the markers are gone, and staging whatever else happened to be sitting in the working tree at the same time.

git add --resolved is supposed to fix that. It stages only the paths git still considers unmerged, and it is meant to refuse if any of those paths still contain leftover conflict markers. I built it from source, because the Ubuntu 24.04 container I was working in only had 2.43.0, and ran it against a handful of conflicts I created on purpose.

The core promise held up. The safety check around it had a gap I didn't expect.

Setting it up

Git 2.56.0 isn't in Ubuntu's repositories yet, so I built it from the kernel.org tarball:

$ ./configure --prefix=$HOME/git-2.56
$ make -j4 NO_GETTEXT=1 NO_TCLTK=1 NO_CURL=1
$ make install NO_GETTEXT=1 NO_TCLTK=1 NO_CURL=1
$ ./git-2.56/bin/git --version
git version 2.56.0

I skipped curl and gettext support because the testing only needed local commands. git add -h confirmed the flag is there:

    --[no-]resolved       add conflict-resolved tracked files

The core promise: it does ignore unrelated files

I built a repo with two branches that both edit file1.txt and file2.txt, merged them to force a conflict, resolved both files properly, and then made an unrelated edit to a third file, file4.txt, that had nothing to do with the merge.

Command file1.txt (resolved) file2.txt (resolved) file4.txt (unrelated edit)
git add . staged staged staged
git add --resolved . staged staged left unstaged

That's the whole pitch, and it's real. After git add --resolved ., git status --short showed:

M  file1.txt
M  file2.txt
 M file4.txt

The leading column is the staged state and the second is the working-tree state. file4.txt has a space in the first column, meaning nothing about it is staged. With plain git add . on the same working tree, all three files come back M in the index column. If you've ever committed a stray console.log or a half-finished change because it happened to be sitting in the tree during a conflict resolution, this removes that failure mode outright.

What it refuses, and what I got wrong on the way

The second claim is that --resolved checks the paths it's about to stage for leftover <<<<<<< markers and aborts if it finds any. My first attempt to test this looked like it had found a bug: I resolved one file, left markers in the other on purpose, ran the command, and got exit code 0 with nothing printed and nothing staged.

That looked like a silent no-op where the documentation promised an error. It wasn't. The problem was my test harness, not the flag. In the run before that one, I had already run git add --resolved . successfully once on that same working tree and then called git reset to put things back for the next scenario. git reset rewrites the index against HEAD, and in doing so it collapses the unmerged (stage 1/2/3) entries into ordinary staged-then-unstaged entries. By the time I reintroduced the markers, git no longer considered those paths unmerged at all, so --resolved had nothing to look at and correctly did nothing. I was testing a file that looked conflicted to a human and wasn't conflicted to git.

Once I rebuilt the conflict from scratch instead of reusing a reset repo, the refusal showed up exactly as documented:

$ git add --resolved .
fatal: the following paths still have conflict markers:
    file2.txt

Exit code 128. And it's atomic: file1.txt was fully and correctly resolved in that same run, but it stayed UU in the index alongside the broken file2.txt. --resolved does not partially stage the paths it's happy with; one bad file blocks the whole invocation. Only after I actually removed the markers from file2.txt did the second run stage both files.

The gap: the check only applies while git calls a file unmerged

The accidental discovery above pointed at something real, so I tested it on purpose. I merged two branches with one conflicting file, left the file with genuine, un-removed <<<<<<< markers, and ran git add --resolved -v . against it while there was no merge in progress and no unmerged entry for that path at all — just an ordinary tracked file with marker text sitting inside it from an earlier git reset.

$ git status --short
 M file1.txt
$ git add --resolved -v .
$ echo exit: $?
exit: 0

No output, even with -v. Nothing staged. The file still contains real <<<<<<< and ======= and >>>>>>> lines, and --resolved walked straight past it, because the only thing it checks is whether the path is in conflict stages in the index right now, not whether the file's content looks like a conflict. The marker scan is a guard on top of "this file is still unmerged," not a general scan for marker text in tracked files. If you've already run any add/reset sequence that clears the unmerged bit — including, ironically, a first successful use of --resolved itself followed by amending something — the safety net is gone and the next --resolved call will happily do nothing, silently, on a file that still has markers in it.

The other gap: it doesn't look inside a file

I then resolved a conflict and, in the same edit, added one extra unrelated line to the same file, to see whether --resolved could tell the two apart:

 line1
 main change
+A change
+UNRELATED DEBUG LINE I FORGOT TO REMOVE

git add --resolved . staged this without complaint. The flag's unit of "unrelated" is the file, not the line. It stops you from staging file4.txt because it's a different path. It will not stop you from staging a debug line you left in the middle of the file you were actually supposed to be fixing.

What it costs

I timed git add --resolved . against plain git add . on a repo with 3,000 genuinely conflicting files, all pre-resolved, five runs each:

Run add --resolved add
1 0.202s 0.196s
2 0.223s 1.404s
3 0.202s 0.230s
4 0.439s 0.168s
5 0.820s 0.175s

The spread swamps the difference. I expected scanning every conflicted file's content for marker strings to show up as a consistent tax on top of ordinary staging, and it didn't: the two distributions overlap, and the single slowest run in the whole table (1.4s) belongs to plain add, not --resolved. On this machine, at this scale, the marker check is not a cost worth worrying about.

Run it yourself 

#!/bin/bash
set -e
GIT=/path/to/git-2.56/bin/git
$GIT init -q -b main repo && cd repo
$GIT config user.email t@t.com && $GIT config user.name T
echo base > a.txt; echo base > b.txt
$GIT add . && $GIT commit -q -m base
$GIT checkout -q -b branchA
echo "A change" >> a.txt; echo "A change" >> b.txt
$GIT commit -q -am branchA
$GIT checkout -q main
echo "main change" >> a.txt; echo "main change" >> b.txt
echo "unrelated edit" >> c.txt
$GIT commit -q -am main
set +e
$GIT merge branchA  # conflicts in a.txt and b.txt
set -e

# resolve a.txt and b.txt by hand:
printf "base\nmain change\nA change\n" > a.txt
printf "base\nmain change\nA change\n" > b.txt

$GIT add --resolved .
$GIT status --short   # c.txt stays unstaged

I ran this exact sequence while writing the post and it produces the table above.

What to do with this

If your merge workflow still ends in git add ., switching to git add --resolved removes a real failure mode: unrelated dirty files no longer ride along into the merge commit, for free, with no measurable cost. Don't treat the marker check as a general-purpose guard against committing broken conflict markers, though. It only fires while git's index still thinks the path is unmerged. If you've run any sequence that clears that state — a reset, an aborted add, a rebase that re-touches the same path — check the file yourself before you commit, because --resolved will not catch it, and it will not tell you it didn't.

articles.title: Rust Doesn't Have a Garbage Collector. It Has Something Stranger.
articles.description: A visual guide to how Rust's compiler proves your memory is safe before your program ever runs. No garbage collector, no manual free(), no runtime cost.
articles.body_html:
Every language you have used solves the same problem: who cleans up the memory?

In C, the answer is you. You call malloc, you call free, and if you forget, your program leaks memory until it crashes. If you free too early, you get a use-after-free bug, the kind of vulnerability that has caused real-world security exploits for three decades.

In Java, Python, and Go, the answer is a garbage collector. A background process scans your heap at runtime, finds objects nobody points to anymore, and reclaims their memory. It works, but it comes at a cost: unpredictable pauses, extra CPU cycles, and a runtime that your compiled binary must carry everywhere.

Rust looked at both approaches and said: neither.

Rust has no garbage collector. It also does not ask you to manually free memory. Instead, the Rust compiler mathematically proves, before your program ever runs, that every piece of memory will be freed at exactly the right moment, exactly once, with zero runtime overhead.

The mechanism behind this is called the ownership system, and it is unlike anything in mainstream programming.

The Three Rules That Replace a Garbage Collector

Rust's entire memory model rests on three rules enforced at compile time:

  1. Every value in Rust has exactly one owner.
  2. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped (its memory is freed).
  3. You can temporarily borrow a value, but the compiler tracks every borrow to make sure nothing conflicts.

That sounds simple. Almost suspiciously simple. But these three rules are powerful enough to prevent use-after-free, double-free, dangling pointers, and data races, all without a single byte of runtime overhead.

Let us see exactly how.

Rule 1: One Owner, One Cleanup Responsibility

Consider this Rust code:

fn main() {
    let s = String::from("hello");
    let s2 = s;
    println!("{}", s); // ← This line will NOT compile.
}

If you come from Python or JavaScript, that code looks perfectly fine. You made a string, assigned it to another variable, and tried to print the original. What could go wrong?

In Rust, this fails to compile with the error:

error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `s`

Here is what happened. String::from("hello") allocated memory on the heap to store the text. The variable s became the owner of that heap allocation. When you wrote let s2 = s, Rust did not copy the heap data. It moved ownership from s to s2.

After the move, s is no longer valid. The compiler marks it as dead. If you try to use s after the move, the compiler refuses, because allowing that would create two variables pointing at the same heap memory, and when both go out of scope, the runtime would try to free the same block twice.

This is the key insight: Rust does not need a garbage collector because ownership makes the cleanup point deterministic. The compiler knows exactly when each value's owner leaves scope, so it inserts the deallocation call right there, automatically, at compile time.

Rule 2: Borrowing Instead of Sharing

If ownership always moved, Rust would be unusable. Every function call would consume its arguments.

So Rust lets you borrow a value using references:

fn print_length(s: &String) {
    println!("Length: {}", s.len());
}

fn main() {
    let s = String::from("hello");
    print_length(&s);       // Borrow s, don't move it.
    println!("{}", s);       // s is still valid here.
}

The & symbol creates a reference, a temporary, read-only view of the data. The function print_length borrows s but does not own it. When print_length returns, the borrow ends, and s remains valid in main.

But here is where Rust gets strict. The compiler enforces a fundamental aliasing rule:

At any given time, you can have either one mutable reference or any number of immutable references. Never both.

fn main() {
    let mut s = String::from("hello");

    let r1 = &s;       // Immutable borrow — fine.
    let r2 = &s;       // Another immutable borrow — still fine.
    let r3 = &mut s;   // Mutable borrow — COMPILE ERROR.
}

Why does the compiler care? Because this rule prevents data races at compile time. If two parts of your code could read a value while a third part is modifying it, the program behavior becomes unpredictable. Languages with garbage collectors allow this and rely on the programmer to add locks. Rust makes it structurally impossible.

What the Compiler Actually Builds

Most tutorials stop at the rules. But understanding how the compiler enforces those rules reveals why the system works with zero runtime cost.

When you run cargo build, your Rust source code passes through a pipeline of transformations:

The critical stage is MIR, the Mid-level Intermediate Representation. Before your code reaches MIR, the compiler has already parsed the syntax (AST), desugared complex expressions (HIR), and resolved all types. But ownership and borrowing have not been checked yet.

MIR represents your program as a control-flow graph: a network of basic blocks connected by branches. Each block contains simple, flat statements. No nested expressions, no hidden control flow.

Here is a simplified view of what MIR looks like for a small function:

bb0: {
    _1 = String::from("hello")   // allocate
    _2 = move _1                 // ownership transfers
    drop(_2)                     // compiler inserts cleanup
    return
}

Notice the word move. In MIR, every ownership transfer is explicit. The compiler can now walk this graph and track exactly which variable owns each value at every point in the program.

This is where the borrow checker runs. It performs dataflow analysis on the MIR, tracing every value's lifetime, every borrow's span, and every move. If the analysis finds a conflict, it rejects the program with a compile error.

If no conflicts exist, the compiler knows something powerful: every value will be freed exactly once, at a known location, and no reference will ever outlive its data.

The safety proof is complete. Everything after this point is pure optimization.

The "Zero-Cost" Part: What Reaches the CPU

After the borrow checker approves your code, the MIR is translated into LLVM IR and handed to the LLVM optimization engine, the same backend used by Clang for C and C++.

By this point, the ownership rules have already been enforced. LLVM does not know or care about Rust's borrow checker. It sees ordinary code with explicit allocation and deallocation points, and it optimizes the result like any other systems language.

Consider this function:

fn sum_lengths(a: &str, b: &str) -> usize {
    a.len() + b.len()
}

No heap allocation. No reference counting. No garbage collector scan. The compiler verifies the borrows at compile time, and the generated machine code is a plain addition of two integers. The abstraction evaporated completely.

This is what Rust means by "zero-cost abstractions": the safety checks happen during compilation and leave no trace in the final binary. Your program runs as fast as an equivalent C program, but the compiler has already proven it cannot corrupt memory.

Lifetimes: The Compiler's Invisible Bookkeeping

Sometimes the borrow checker needs help figuring out how long a reference should live. That is where lifetime annotations appear:

fn longer<'a>(s1: &'a str, s2: &'a str) -> &'a str {
    if s1.len() > s2.len() { s1 } else { s2 }
}

The 'a annotation does not change your program's behavior. It is a hint to the borrow checker: "the returned reference lives at least as long as both input references."

This lets the compiler verify, at compile time, that the caller does not use the returned reference after either s1 or s2 has been freed. If it cannot prove safety, it refuses to compile.

Lifetime annotations are not runtime markers. They are erased during compilation, just like the ownership checks. They exist only to help the compiler complete its proof.

Most of the time, you never write them. Rust has lifetime elision rules that infer the common patterns automatically. You only need explicit annotations when the compiler genuinely cannot determine the relationships on its own.

When Ownership Is Not Enough

Rust's ownership system covers the vast majority of programs, but it has limits. Some data structures, like graphs or doubly-linked lists, require multiple owners by design. The compiler's single-owner rule would make them impossible to express.

For these cases, Rust provides opt-in runtime mechanisms:

  • Rc<T> (Reference Counting): Tracks the number of owners at runtime. When the count reaches zero, the value is dropped. Single-threaded only.
  • Arc<T> (Atomic Reference Counting): Like Rc, but safe to share across threads using atomic operations.
  • RefCell<T>: Moves borrow checking from compile time to runtime. Panics if you violate the aliasing rules.

These types carry a small runtime cost, which is why they are explicit and opt-in. Rust does not hide the cost. You choose exactly where to pay it, and the compiler enforces everything else for free.

Why This Matters Beyond Rust

The ownership model is not just a language feature. It represents a fundamentally different answer to a problem every programmer faces.

C and C++ gave the programmer full control and full responsibility. Entire classes of security vulnerabilities, buffer overflows, use-after-free, dangling pointers, exist because humans make mistakes with manual memory management. Microsoft estimated that roughly 70% of their security vulnerabilities were caused by memory safety issues.

Garbage-collected languages solved safety by adding a runtime process. That works, but it introduces latency spikes, higher memory usage, and a floor on performance that no amount of tuning can fully remove.

Rust found a third path: prove safety at compile time and generate code with no overhead. The tradeoff is compilation time and a steeper learning curve. The borrow checker requires you to think about data ownership explicitly, something that most languages let you ignore.

But once you internalize the model, the compiler stops being an obstacle and starts acting as a collaborator that catches entire categories of bugs before your code ever executes.

If you have tried Rust and hit a wall with the borrow checker, try looking at it from the compiler's perspective. It is not being difficult. It is building a mathematical proof that your program cannot corrupt memory, and it is asking you for enough information to finish that proof. Once you see the errors through that lens, they start making sense.

What was the first Rust compiler error that genuinely surprised you? And if you have not tried Rust yet, what is the one thing that still feels intimidating about it?

References:

  • The Rust Programming Language, Chapter 4: Understanding Ownership (Official Rust Book)
  • Rust Compiler Development Guide: MIR
  • Rust Compiler Development Guide: The Borrow Checker
  • Microsoft Security Response Center: Memory Safety (70% of CVEs are memory safety issues)
