articles.title: C# Without a Project File: File-Based Apps in .NET 11 (a 5-Minute Refresh)
articles.description: Since .NET 10 you can run a C# file without a project: dotnet run app.cs. No .sln, no .csproj. But it...
articles.body_html:
Since .NET 10 you can run a C# file without a project: dotnet run app.cs. No .sln, no .csproj. But it was one file only. In .NET 11 a file-based app can have many files, and that makes it useful for real small tools.

I tried it on the classic Mars Rover kata. A rover starts at 0 0 N. L and R turn 90°, M moves one cell forward. The program prints the final position.


The real Mars rover: Perseverance, with the Ingenuity helicopter behind it. Ours only knows L, R and M. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS

Here is what we'll go through:

  1. One file: run C# without a project
  2. #:include: split the app into files
  3. Nested includes: a file that includes other files
  4. Settings: read a JSON file, and watch it crash
  5. Native AOT: turn it off, or use the JSON source generator

1. One file: run C# without a project 

// app.cs
Console.WriteLine("Rover is ready");

dotnet run app.cs

That's all. The SDK creates a hidden project for you.

2. #:include: split the app into files

Move the rover logic to its own file, and include it from app.cs:

mars-rover/
├── app.cs
├── settings.json
├── rover/rover.cs
└── helpers/directions.cs

// app.cs
#:include rover/rover.cs

var rover = new Rover(0, 0, "N");
rover.Execute("LMLMLMLMM");
Console.WriteLine(rover);   // 0 1 N

One rule: only the entry file (app.cs) can have top-level statements. Included files only add types.

3. Nested includes: a file that includes other files

The rover includes the directions helper itself, so app.cs doesn't need to know about it:

// rover/rover.cs
#:include ../helpers/directions.cs

class Rover(int x, int y, string facing)
{
    int _x = x, _y = y;
    int _dir = Directions.IndexOf(facing);

    public void Execute(string commands)
    {
        foreach (var c in commands)
        {
            switch (c)
            {
                case 'L': _dir = Directions.Left(_dir); break;
                case 'R': _dir = Directions.Right(_dir); break;
                case 'M':
                    var (dx, dy) = Directions.Delta(_dir);
                    _x += dx; _y += dy;
                    break;
                default: throw new ArgumentException($"Unknown command: {c}");
            }
        }
    }

    public override string ToString() => $"{_x} {_y} {Directions.Name(_dir)}";
}

// helpers/directions.cs
static class Directions
{
    const string Ring = "NESW";   // clockwise
    static readonly (int, int)[] Deltas = [(0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0)];

    public static int IndexOf(string f) =>
        Ring.IndexOf(f) is var i and >= 0 && f.Length == 1 ? i : throw new ArgumentException($"Unknown direction: {f}");

    public static int Left(int d) => (d + 3) % 4;
    public static int Right(int d) => (d + 1) % 4;
    public static (int, int) Delta(int d) => Deltas[d];
    public static char Name(int d) => Ring[d];
}

Each file says what it needs, like a using, but for files.

4. Settings: read a JSON file, and watch it crash

Put the start position in settings.json:

{ "X": 0, "Y": 0, "Facing": "N" }

Read it from the folder of app.cs, so it works wherever you run the app from:

var dir = AppContext.GetData("EntryPointFileDirectoryPath") as string ?? ".";
var json = File.ReadAllText(Path.Combine(dir, "settings.json"));
var start = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<Start>(json)!;

record Start(int X, int Y, string Facing);

Run it, and it crashes:

System.InvalidOperationException:
Reflection-based serialization has been disabled for this application.

5. Native AOT: turn it off, or use the JSON source generator

File-based apps have Native AOT on by default, and AOT turns off reflection-based JSON. You have two options.

Option A: turn AOT off. Add one line at the top, and the code from step 4 works as is:

#:property PublishAot=false

Option B: keep AOT, use the JSON source generator. A few more lines, but you keep the fast startup and the native binary:

#!/usr/bin/env dotnet
#:include rover/rover.cs

using System.Text.Json;
using System.Text.Json.Serialization;

var dir = AppContext.GetData("EntryPointFileDirectoryPath") as string ?? ".";
var json = File.ReadAllText(Path.Combine(dir, "settings.json"));
var start = JsonSerializer.Deserialize(json, AppJson.Default.Start)!;

var rover = new Rover(start.X, start.Y, start.Facing);
rover.Execute(args.Length > 0 ? args[0] : "LMLMLMLMM");
Console.WriteLine(rover);

record Start(int X, int Y, string Facing);

[JsonSerializable(typeof(Start))]
partial class AppJson : JsonSerializerContext;

$ dotnet run app.cs
0 1 N
$ dotnet run app.cs -- RRMMLM
1 -2 E

For a quick tool, A is fine. If startup time matters, choose B. The #! line on top removes analyzer warning CA2266, and on macOS/Linux it lets you run chmod +x app.cs && ./app.cs.

Notes for later

  1. dotnet run app.cs runs a C# file without a project.
  2. #:include path.cs adds another file (.NET 11).
  3. Included files can include other files. Only the entry file has top-level code.
  4. EntryPointFileDirectoryPath gives you the folder of your app file.
  5. AOT is on by default: use #:property PublishAot=false or the JSON source generator.

Would you use this for small tools, or stay with projects? Tell me in comments. 🙂

articles.title: This GitHub Repo Gives You 100+ AI Agents for Different Jobs
articles.description: If you've been scrolling through X or GitHub lately, you've probably seen msitarzewski/agency-agents...
articles.body_html:
If you've been scrolling through X or GitHub lately, you've probably seen msitarzewski/agency-agents pop up in your feed. Whenever a repo starts trending like this, people usually hype it up like it's some brand new AI breakthrough, so to be clear upfront: it's not a new model, a runtime framework, or a standalone coding tool. It's literally just a public repository full of markdown files containing detailed system prompts.

That said, once you look past the hype, it's actually pretty useful—especially if you're tired of writing your own custom instructions from scratch or if your coding assistant keeps agreeing with every bad architectural idea you throw at it.

What's actually in the repo

Most prompt repositories on GitHub are filled with generic one-liners like "act as a senior engineer and write clean code." Those rarely change how an LLM behaves once you get past the first two messages.

agency-agents takes a different approach by organizing over a hundred multi-page markdown files into clear categories (engineering, testing, design, product, etc.). Instead of vague encouragement, each file outlines specific rules, edge cases to watch out for, formatting expectations, and explicit instructions on when the model should push back.

For example, if you're refactoring a messy script or designing a new data pipeline, you can load up the reality-checker.md or software-architect.md file. Instead of blindly generating boilerplate and telling you every idea is great, the model actually critiques your structure, points out potential bottlenecks, and forces you to simplify things before writing code.

How to set it up locally

Since everything in the repo is just plain text, there are no dependencies to install, no Docker containers to spin up, and no background daemons eating RAM. You just clone the repository somewhere permanent on your machine and point whatever tool you already use to the specific file you need.

1. Clone the repo locally 

git clone https://github.com/msitarzewski/agency-agents.git ~/.local/share/agency-agents

2. Pick a file and wire it into your tool

Depending on your workflow, you just symlink or copy the markdown file into your project directory:

  • Claude Code / CLI workflows: Symlink the file to CLAUDE.md in your project root so it loads automatically when you start a session (just make sure to add CLAUDE.md to your .gitignore if you're working on a shared repo): 
  ln -s ~/.local/share/agency-agents/engineering/software-architect.md ./CLAUDE.md
  • Cursor / Windsurf: Copy or symlink the .md file straight into your project's .cursor/rules/ directory.
  • Local models (Ollama / llama.cpp): If you run models locally in the terminal, you can pass the file contents directly into your system prompt flag: 
  llama-cli -m your-model.gguf --system-prompt "$(cat ~/.local/share/agency-agents/testing/reality-checker.md)" -p "Review this code"
  • Neovim / Editor plugins: If you use local AI plugins like Avante, CodeCompanion, or similar setups, you can simply point your custom system prompt path to whichever .md file fits the task you're working on.

(There's also a small Tauri app called agency-agents-app linked in the repo if you prefer clicking through a GUI to copy them into your editor configs, though symlinking in the terminal takes two seconds).

A practical way to use it without clutter

The easiest mistake to make with a repo this big is trying to combine multiple personas at once or keeping a heavy system prompt active all the time.

A better workflow is swapping them out depending on what phase of a project you're in. Use a planning or architecture persona when you're mapping out how components talk to each other, switch to a standard implementation prompt while writing the actual functions, and then swap in a testing or reality-checker file right before you commit to catch edge cases you missed. Because they're just symlinks, switching roles takes a single terminal command.

Worth keeping in mind

At the end of the day, it's still just prompt engineering. If you're running a smaller local model with a tight context window, loading a 2,000-word markdown file will eat up a noticeable chunk of your token budget before you even paste your code. It works best when you pick one focused role for the exact problem in front of you, or trim down the markdown files to keep only the rules relevant to your stack.

Curious if anyone else here keeps a local folder of system prompts like this, or if you've found better repos worth cloning.

Interested in collaborating?

If you're a company or team working in AI or developer technology, I'd love to hear about what you're building. I'm always interested in discovering new projects and sharing technologies that I genuinely find useful with my readers.

You can reach me at maamrihayder@gmail.com.

articles.title: Debugging SQL Should Be Just Like Debugging Code
articles.description: Debugging SQL is still mostly guesswork   Suppose you run an 80-line SQL query and discover...
articles.body_html:
Debugging SQL is still mostly guesswork

Suppose you run an 80-line SQL query and discover that one of the result columns contains incorrect numbers. What’s your first instinct? Run it again.

At this point, a programmer would open the debugger, set breakpoints, and step through the code. They could see exactly how each variable changes and what value it holds at every step. What about SQL developers? They can only stare at the final result and guess: Is the join condition wrong? Does a window function miss a partition? You want to see the result of an intermediate step? You can’t. You have to split the CTEs and even the nested queries, one by one, turn them into standalone SELECT statements, run them individually, and then piece everything back together.

This isn’t debugging – this is archeology.

SQL debugging is still stuck at “run it, then stare at the output and guess.”

You’d never accept this way of debugging when write code – so why do you put up with it when you write SQL?

A real-world scenario: finding a neighboring record by offset

That’s all abstract. Let’s look a concrete example.

A workshop scan log table records, in each row, the cardboard sheet number scanned at a certain moment on a certain production line. The requirement: group by production line and sort by time within each group. Then find the records whose number equals a given string (for example, spL1ml82N4o), together with the 2 records before and the 2 records after each one, and finally remove duplicates by id.

Written in traditional SQL (MySQL), it looks like this:

SELECT id,
  MAX(Cardboard_Number) AS Cardboard_Number,
  MAX(date_Time) AS date_Time,
  MAX(ProductionLine_Number) AS ProductionLine_Number,
  MAX(flag) AS flag,
  MAX(in_range) AS in_range
FROM (
  SELECT id, Cardboard_Number, date_Time, ProductionLine_Number, flag, in_range
  FROM (
    SELECT id, Cardboard_Number, date_Time, ProductionLine_Number,
      MAX(flag) OVER (
        PARTITION BY ProductionLine_Number
        ORDER BY ProductionLine_Number ASC, date_Time ASC
        ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND 2 FOLLOWING) AS in_range
    FROM (
      SELECT id, Cardboard_Number, date_Time, ProductionLine_Number,
        CASE WHEN Cardboard_Number = 'spL1ml82N4o' THEN 1 END AS flag
      FROM table1
    ) AS flagged
  ) AS marked
  WHERE in_range = 1
) AS filtered
GROUP BY id;.

We won’t explain this code line by line, only what it looks like: three layers of nested derived tables, with flagging, window frame, filtering, and distinct all crammed into one query. Every layer has to list the fields all over again, and to see an intermediate result, all you can do is keep breaking it apart from the inside.

The real problem isn’t that the SQL is hard to read. It’s that it’s hard to debug. The most fragile part of this SQL is the window frame: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND 2 FOLLOWING. If you get the offsets wrong, it won’t throw an error. If you leave out a segmentation key, it won’t throw an error either. It will simply produce slightly incorrect results, silently. The output looks almost right, but not quite – the kind of result that makes your palms sweat just before deployment. And the intermediate flag columns and window-match indicator columns aren’t included in the final output at all. If you can’t see them, you can’t validate whether they’re correct.

SQLazy: Write step by step, debug one step at a time

What if we took a different approach? Instead of delivering a single SQL query as the final product, we break the logic into steps, each of which can be executed and its result inspected.

That’s exactly what SQLazy does. SQLazy is an intuitive, easy-to-understand language for structured data processing. It breaks logic into clear steps, produces deterministic output, and makes the entire process easy to audit. The same task takes just five steps in SQLazy:


It also has a dedicated debugging feature: single-step execution. Click once and it runs one step. and the result tables of the current step and all the steps before it are there for you to browse at any time. This is the same thing as the single-stepping you use when debugging Python or Java. The only difference is that SQLazy’s code structure is simpler, with no branches, loops or subroutines, so you don’t need breakpoints, step in and step out routine. Every statement is already one step.

Back to the task above, here’s what the debugging experience looks like:

  • Step 1: Sorting: click a group and check whether the order is right;

  • Step 2: Flag the target rows and check whether any have been missed.

  • Step 3: Retrieve the two preceding and two following rows. This is the most error-prone part of the entire query, where both the window frame and segmentation keys come into play. Step through the query to this point and inspect the in_range column. You can see at a glance which rows matched and which didn’t.

  • Step 4: Filter the rows.

  • Step 5: Remove duplicates. Just click each step to inspect its result.

In SQL, a mistake in the window frame leaves you guessing. In SQLazy, just step through to Step 3 and inspect the results.

If something goes wrong, just fix the step where the error occurs – there’s no need to rewrite the entire query from scratch. Once you’ve verified that the logic is correct, you can also execute all the steps with a single click, letting them run in sequence to produce the final result.

It’s a change in form, not just syntax

Someone might argue, “Can’t I just run a SELECT on each CTE in SQL to inspect the intermediate results?” Yes, you can. But that’s manual, makeshift step-by-step debugging. Every time the logic changes, you have to split the query again. Those steps aren’t saved for you. AI can’t fix this either. What AI writes for you is still one final SQL statement. If something goes wrong, you’re back to guessing from scratch.

AI writes the logic. A compiler writes the SQL.

In SQLazy, AI plans the business logic as a sequence of steps, and the compiler compiles these steps into native SQL. The steps are for human to read and debug, and the SQL is for machines to run. Each has its own job.

he compiled SQL is equivalent to what you’d write by hand. There’s no extra abstraction layer – j you can copy it and use it as is, and it isn’t tied to any particular database.

To be honest, for simple CRUD, just write the SQL directly. You don’t need SQLazy for that. What really deserves step-by-step debugging is logic where one wrong step spoils everything – things like grouping records to find the neighbor, condition-based resets, and segment-based alignment.

A different approach to debugging

Want to try the step-by-step execution? Visit https://www.sqlazy.com/?2Qkto run this example of searching for adjacent records by offset.

You can also visit our example library (https://github.com/SPLWare/SQLazy/tree/master/examples) to find more examples about sessionization, continuous interval, and dynamic grouped reports.

How do you usually find errors when you debug SQL? Break the CTEs apart and run them one by one, or stare at the output and think hard? Either way, it’s more tiring than clicking single-step execution.

articles.title: I Served a Map of Dhaka From One 17 MB File — Tiles Came Back in 1.1 ms.
articles.description: Self-hosting your own map tiles used to mean running a tile server, a database, and a bill you had to...
articles.body_html:
Self-hosting your own map tiles used to mean running a tile server, a database, and a bill you had to watch. The claim going around this week is that it got cheap and easy: one file, no server worth naming, no key, no per-view charge. I wanted to see how true that is, so I picked a city I know, Dhaka, cut it out of the planet, and served it from my own laptop. The whole thing took about ten minutes of actual work, and the numbers are better than the claim.

Cutting Dhaka out of the planet

Protomaps builds the whole of OpenStreetMap into a single file every day. The full planet build is about 140 GB. Nobody downloads that. The point of the format is that you cut out just the piece you need, and the tool only downloads the bytes belonging to your piece.

I took the November 15 build and asked for Dhaka, a box from 90.30 to 90.50 east and 23.70 to 23.90 north, roughly the city centre and its edges. The tool came back with 578 tiles and a file of 17,797,402 bytes, about 17 MB. It took 35.5 seconds and 53 small downloads adding up to 19 MB, because the tool pulls the index first and then only the chunks holding my tiles. Nineteen megabytes in, 17 out, and the planet file never crossed my machine in full.

That ratio is the whole pitch, stated as a number. The planet is about 140 GB. My city is 17 MB. That is roughly eight thousand times smaller, for a map that covers the place I actually wanted. If you run a site about one city, one region, one trail, you are not in the planet business at all. You are in the 17 MB business.

The file itself checks out. It is a version 3 archive, vector tiles, zoom levels 0 to 15, gzip-compressed, built from OpenStreetMap data as of November 15 at 04:00 UTC. I ran the format's own verify step over it and it came back clean. The map data inside is a day old. If a road changes tomorrow, my file does not know about it until I cut a fresh one. That is the trade, and I will come back to it.

Serving it: one command, 148 milliseconds

Serving the file took one command and no configuration. The tool starts a small tile server on your machine, and the first tile came back 148 milliseconds after I started it. No database to start, no cache to warm, no config file to write.

Then I asked it for 27 tiles: nine spots around Dhaka at zooms 5 through 15, each one three times. Every single one came back with a 200. The middle of the pack, the median, was 1.1 milliseconds. The average was 4.3. The slowest was 31.4 milliseconds, and that was the very first request for the zoom-5 tile, before the cache had anything in it. Every warm request after that landed between 0.7 and 1.3 milliseconds. On a plain laptop, on a local network, a map tile is about a millisecond of work.

The tiles themselves are not all the same size. The smallest I asked for was 1,254 bytes, a quiet corner at zoom 15. The biggest was 107,624 bytes, the city centre at zoom 12, where every road, building and label in central Dhaka is packed into one square. The average was about 44 KB. So a screen full of map at street level is a handful of 40 KB squares, each arriving in about a millisecond. That is the part that surprised me: I expected the format to be clever about storage, and it is, but I did not expect the serving to be this boring. It just answers.

Two more details from the run, because they are the kind of thing you only learn by trying. First, a tile outside my box, one step east of Dhaka at zoom 12, came back empty in 0.65 milliseconds, a 204 with no body. The map outside your cut is not wrong or broken. It is blank. If your readers pan past the edge, they see nothing, and you need a bigger cut or a low-zoom world underneath it. Second, the little TileJSON document the server is supposed to hand out, the one that tells a map library where the tiles live, refused to work until I gave the server a public address. Without it, a 501. That is the one thing in the whole run that did not work out of the box, and it took a minute to understand.

The catch, and it is a real one

Nothing here is wrong. But three things are worth knowing before you move your maps to this.

The first is the dead link in the docs. The guides that teach this format point beginners at a demo archive, v4.pmtiles, hosted for testing. When I went to look at it on November 16, it returned a 404. The file is gone, for now at least. If you followed a tutorial this week and your map loaded empty, that may be why, and it is not your fault. Cut your own file instead. It takes 35 seconds.

The second is freshness. A file is a snapshot. OpenStreetMap changes every hour, and my Dhaka file is already a day old. A live tile service updates under you. A file does not. If your map needs today's roads, you need a routine that cuts a fresh file every week or every month, and you need to remember that routine exists. For most small sites, a monthly cut is plenty. For a delivery app, it is not.

The third is size at the edges. A city is 17 MB. A country is hundreds of megabytes to a few gigabytes. The whole planet is 140 GB. The format scales, but your hosting bill and your download time scale with it, and the "one small file" story is really a "one small file for one small place" story. Pick your place honestly.

What it costs, and what it replaces

Here is the comparison that matters. A hosted map tile service charges per view, or per thousand views, and the bill grows with your traffic. A file like this costs whatever your plain file hosting costs, which for 17 MB is nothing, and the traffic it serves is ordinary file traffic. There is no key to rotate, no account to watch, no usage dashboard to check at the end of the month. The map library in the visitor's own page reads the file in pieces, asking only for the parts of it that cover the screen, which is why the whole thing works from plain static hosting in the first place.

That is the real change. Not that maps got cheaper, though they did, but that the moving parts disappeared. The database, the tile server, the cache layer, the key management: all of it collapses into a file you can copy, back up, and serve from anywhere that serves files. I built this on a laptop in an evening. A city map, 17 MB, tiles in a millisecond, no bill attached.

If you run anything with a map on it, a shop finder, a trail guide, a local history page, try cutting your own place first. Thirty-five seconds and 19 MB will tell you whether the claim holds for you. For Dhaka, it held.

articles.title: Your .npmrc Says Ignore-Scripts. The Repo's .npmrc Says Otherwise — and the Repo Wins
articles.description: I added one line to my own npm config a few months ago and stopped worrying about install hooks. The...
articles.body_html:
I added one line to my own npm config a few months ago and stopped worrying about install hooks. The line was ignore-scripts=true, sitting in my user-level .npmrc, and in my head it worked like a lock on my front door. Any package I installed could bring whatever code it wanted in its install step, and my machine would just refuse to run it. That was the deal I thought I'd made with npm.

Then cryptostrapon asked a question in the comments on the install-hooks piece that I couldn't answer from memory. If a repo ships its own .npmrc that says ignore-scripts=false, does that beat my setting? I had a guess. My guess was wrong in the direction that matters, so I ran the test instead of arguing from memory.

The test was small on purpose. I built a package with one preinstall hook and nothing else. The hook writes a small marker file with a timestamp and prints a line, and the package itself does nothing at all. Then I installed it three ways on my own machine, node v24.22.1 and npm 10.9.4, and checked for the marker file after each install. The marker file is the whole test. If it's there, the hook ran. If it's not, it didn't.

Problem 1: the repo outranks you.

npm reads its config in layers, and the project layer sits on top. A .npmrc in the project folder beats the one in your home folder, which beats the global one, which beats the built-in defaults. I knew this in the abstract. I had never watched it eat my own safety setting.

First install: only my user config in play, ignore-scripts=true, no repo config at all. I asked npm what the effective value was and it said true. The install finished, and there was no marker file. The hook stayed silent. So far, the lock worked.

Second install: same user config, untouched. The only change was a repo .npmrc with one line in it, ignore-scripts=false. I asked npm for the effective value again and it said false. My own setting, in my own home folder, had just lost a vote I didn't know was happening. The install finished, and this time the marker file was there, timestamped 2026-11-17T00:07:40Z. The hook had run. I ran that second install again later to keep a clean copy of the marker as evidence, and it wrote a fresh one at 00:08:49Z. Same result twice.

That is the shape of the problem. Your personal setting is not a lock. It's a default, and a default is exactly the kind of thing a project folder is allowed to replace. One line in a repo you just cloned can switch your protection off, and the file that does it sits in plain sight in the repo root, in a file most of us never open before installing.

And before anyone pictures a villain: most repos that set ignore-scripts=false are not trying anything. Plenty of them do it for a boring, legitimate reason. Native packages and build tools often need their install hooks to finish setup, and a repo that sets the value to false is usually just making sure a fresh clone works the first time for everyone. The setting is doing its job. The problem is that the same file, with the same one line, is also the whole attack surface, and nothing in the process distinguishes a helpful repo from a hostile one. Your user config can't tell the difference either. It just loses.

Problem 2: nothing tells you it happened.

This is the part that bothered me more than the override itself. The two installs looked identical from the outside. Both printed the same calm line, "added 1 package". The second one even swallowed the hook's own printed line. The hook ran, wrote its file, and npm showed me nothing about it. I only knew because I went looking for the marker file on purpose.

Think about what that means for a real install. You clone something, you run the install, the output looks normal, and a hook you believed you'd blocked has already run. There is no warning, no yellow text, no hint that your setting lost. The tool did exactly what its config layers told it to do. It just never told you which layer won.

I keep coming back to that silence, because it breaks the one feedback loop that would save you. If npm printed one line, something like "project config turned install hooks back on", the whole issue would be a footnote. You'd see it, shrug, and decide for yourself. Instead the decision happens in a file you didn't write, in a layer you didn't know was voting, and the output looks the same either way. A protection that fails silently is worse than no protection at all, because the silent one still lets you feel safe.

Problem 3: the command-line flag is the only setting that's actually yours.

Third install: same repo config, still saying false, but this time I added --ignore-scripts to the install command itself. The hook stayed silent. No marker file. The flag beat the repo file, the way the repo file had beaten my user config.

That ordering is the honest picture. A flag you type wins over every file. A file in the project wins over a file in your home folder. A file in your home folder only wins when nothing above it has an opinion. Your user config is the weakest voice in that room, and it's the one most of us trust the most.

The catch is obvious, and it's the reason this matters less than it should and more than it does. A flag only protects the install where you remember to type it. Nobody types a flag on every install. We set a config once, forget about it, and trust it forever. That's the whole appeal of a user-level setting, and it's exactly the trust the layering quietly breaks.

So what do I actually do with this now? I stopped treating ignore-scripts=true in my own config as a safety net and started treating it as a preference. For installs I care about, the flag goes on the command. For repos I don't know well, I look at the .npmrc before the install, the same way I'd glance at a package's install hook before running it. It takes ten seconds, and it's the only check that can't be overridden by the thing it's checking. If a repo needs its hooks to build, fine, that's a real reason, and I can decide that with my eyes open instead of finding out afterwards.

Problem 4: the honest limit of this whole test.

Everything above is about install time. A package with no install hook at all can still run code the first time you load it, and no ignore-scripts setting, flag or config file touches that. That's the PolinRider pattern, and I'm not going to pretend I reproduced it here. I didn't. My test package was built to answer one question, whether a repo config beats a user config at install time, and it answered it. The load-time door is a different test, and it deserves its own run before anyone writes about it with confidence.

So the claim stands, and it's a narrower claim than the headline version. Your ignore-scripts setting does protect you, right up until a repo disagrees with it. Then the repo wins, quietly, and the only thing that reliably overrules the repo is a flag you type yourself, every time.

Have you ever caught a repo config undoing something you set for yourself? Not just npm. Any tool where a project file outranked your personal setup and you only found out later. I'd like to hear how you found it, and what you changed after.

articles.title: Longer Timeouts Won't Fix Your Webhook Duplicates. Claiming the Work Once Will
articles.description: The receiver was not down. That is the part I keep coming back to. It was answering every single...
articles.body_html:
The receiver was not down. That is the part I keep coming back to. It was answering every single delivery, taking its time about it, two and a half seconds from first byte to done. My sweeper checked once a second for an acknowledgement, heard nothing after one second, and decided the delivery must be lost. It was not lost. It was still being written down at the other end. By the time the first acknowledgement arrived, the same order had already gone out three times.

That was this morning, on my own machine, with one delivery key and a receiver I had deliberately slowed down. krusenas raised this in the comments on "My Cron Job Fired 50 Times While the Receiver Was Down. 10 Webhooks Vanished." He wanted the slow case, not the dead one. What happens when the receiver is up, healthy, and simply a second too slow for the thing watching it? A dead receiver fails loudly. A slow one looks exactly like a dead one for two and a half seconds, and a sweeper that resends on silence will happily manufacture duplicates out of a delivery that was never in trouble.

Here is the setup, so you can argue with it. One delivery, key evt-1042, a payment confirmation for a single order. A local receiver that sleeps 2.5 seconds before answering 200. A sweeper that ticks every 1.0 second and resends whenever no acknowledgement has arrived. The sender waits up to 4 seconds for each reply, so the first acknowledgement does land, at about 2.5 seconds. I counted duplicates on the receiving side, in the receiver's own log. Then I ran the whole thing twice.

Before the fix After the fix
Sends 3 1
Deliveries the receiver logged 3 1
Extra copies 2 0

Both runs gave the same numbers. Before the fix, the sweeper fired at 0 seconds, at 1 second, and at 2 seconds. The first acknowledgement arrived at 2.5 seconds, a half second after the third copy had already left. After the fix, one send, one delivery, one acknowledgement, and the sweeper spent its next two ticks doing nothing at all. That nothing is the whole point of this piece.

My claim is simple, and I expect some of you to disagree with it. Longer timeouts and longer sweep intervals do not fix webhook duplicates. Only claiming the work once does. Everything else is a new number on the same trap.

Problem 1: silence is not loss

A sweeper that resends on no acknowledgement treats two completely different situations as one. The delivery is gone, or the delivery is slow. From the sender's chair those look identical for the first few seconds. There is no signal in the silence that tells you which one you are in. So the sweeper guesses "lost", because that is the guess a retry loop is built to make. In my run the guess was wrong three times in a row, and each wrong guess was a real copy landing on a real receiver.

People wave this away. "It was only a duplicate, the receiver can ignore it." The receiver in my test was a simple order inbox. It logged three deliveries for one order. If that inbox charges a card, sends a confirmation email, or decrements stock, three deliveries is three of those, unless something downstream catches it. The sweeper created work the receiver never asked for, and then the receiver gets blamed for handling it badly.

Problem 2: the sweeper cannot learn patience from a longer timeout

My first instinct, and probably yours, was to stretch the numbers. Give the sender a longer wait, or the sweeper a longer gap between ticks. I did the arithmetic instead of the change, and the arithmetic is unkind. A 4-second wait already covered the 2.5-second receiver. The timeout was never the problem. The sweeper fired at 1 second and 2 seconds because that is its job: check every second, resend on silence. A longer timeout changes nothing about the second tick.

Stretch the sweep interval instead, say from 1 second to 3 seconds, and this exact receiver stops duplicating. The acknowledgement lands at 2.5 seconds, inside the gap, and the sweeper never fires twice. That feels like a fix. It is a fix for a 2.5-second receiver, on a quiet morning. The next slow day the receiver takes 4 seconds, or 7, or a lock holds it for 12, and the 3-second gap manufactures the same duplicates again. You have not removed the trap. You have moved it to a number you have not hit yet.

Problem 3: every duplicate is a second bill

Count what three deliveries actually cost, even when the receiver is polite enough to ignore two of them. Three sends, three lots of work at the receiving end, three chances for a side effect to slip through. On a busy day that multiplier lands on everything at once, because the slow day is the day every delivery is slow, and the sweeper is resending every one of them. A retry loop that cannot tell slow from lost multiplies the load on the exact receiver that is already struggling, at the exact moment it is struggling. That is a strange way to help.

The fix has to live where the decision lives. The decision is "send this again", and it has to be made once, by one owner, with a record everyone else can see. A longer interval is a hope that the receiver hurries up. A claim is a fact that the work is taken.

Problem 4: a flag in memory is not a claim

The obvious cheap version is a flag in the sender's memory: sending equals true, do not send again. That works until the sender restarts, or until there are two senders, or two copies of the sweeper running side by side, which is exactly how these things end up running. Each one holds its own flag, each one is sure it is the only sender, and the receiver gets two copies anyway. A flag nobody else can see is a private opinion. A claim has to be a shared fact.

So the fix is one row per delivery key, in a table every sender can see, claimed atomically. One row, one key, one owner at a time.

CREATE TABLE claims (
  delivery_key TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  status TEXT,
  claimed_at REAL
);

The sweeper does not check and then claim. It claims, in one step, and the table decides who won. The insert succeeds for the first caller and fails for everyone else, because the key is the primary key and there can only be one row for it. The winner sends. The losers see status in_flight and skip their tick. When the acknowledgement arrives, the winner marks the row done. A slow run cannot be re-claimed while it is in flight, because the row is already there, already owned, already visible to the next tick.

That is the entire change. Same receiver, same 2.5-second delay, same 1-second sweep, same 4-second wait. Three deliveries became one. The sweeper still ticked every second. It just had nothing to do on the second and third ticks, because the row told it the truth the silence could not: this delivery is already being handled.

Two honest limits, because the test was small. First, this was local: one key, one receiver, no real network, no crash in the middle of a send. A claimer that crashes while holding a row would hold it forever unless the row carries a lease that expires, and I did not test a lease. Do not ship a claim without one. Second, the receiver here was slow, never down. The down case was the previous piece. The slow case is the sneakier of the two, because everything looks fine until you count the copies.

If you run webhooks, you have met this bug, probably on a day you were already busy. What did your duplicate cost you, a double charge, a double email, a customer asking why they got three copies of the same thing? And what fixed it for you, a claim like this one, a key check at the receiving end, or something else entirely?

articles.title: Optimizely Web malware (16 Nov 2026): is your snippet clean? A read-only checker with base64 detection
articles.description: 178 organisations served a crypto clipper, card skimmer and iOS exploit loader through their Optimizely Project JavaScript. A bash checker that pulls your snippet, hunts the IOCs (incl. the base64 loader) and grades your CSP, tested on live snippets and fake infected samples.
articles.body_html:
On 16 November 2026, for about 17 hours, malicious JavaScript ran on the websites of 178 organisations: BBC, CNN, Zoom, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Salesforce and more. Their own sites weren't hacked directly. The attacker rewrote customers' Project JavaScript inside Optimizely Web (the A/B testing platform), and Optimizely's CDN served it to everyone.

The payload swapped crypto wallet addresses, skimmed card numbers, exfiltrated cookies and screenshots, and tried to load an exploit chain on older iPhones.

If your company runs Optimizely Web, you want to know whether your snippet is clean now. I wrote a read-only checker script and tested it against live Optimizely snippets and against harmless fake "infected" samples served from a local web server.

What happened (short version)

From Report URI's write-up (linked below), all times UTC:

  • 04:21 first modified snippet (BBC's) loads a webshell.lol script;
  • from 08:28 the main payload is https://1688360.cc/track.js, rebuilt 26 times during the day, with card skimming added at 13:43;
  • 19:24–19:59 186 of 1,611 checked snippets infected;
  • 23:11 all infected Optimizely files cleaned.

The loader showed up in three forms:

  1. a plain injected <script src="https://1688360.cc/track.js">;
  2. the URL hidden in base64 and decoded with atob(), so grepping for 1688360.cc misses it (Smartsheet was cleaned once and re-infected this way);
  3. the full payload inlined and run via eval, as a fallback if 1688360.cc is blocked.

How the attacker got into Optimizely is not public yet.

Who's affected

  • Site owners using Optimizely Web, including those serving the snippet from their own domain (www.example.com/js/<id>.js): the content still comes from the Optimizely project.
  • Visitors on 16 November, especially:
    • anyone who typed a card into a site's own form (hosted payment iframes like Stripe or Adyen were out of reach);
    • anyone who copied or pasted a crypto address;
    • iPhone/iPad on iOS 18.6 or older, which got the Coruna exploit chain. The visible symptom was the page reloading every 60 seconds.

Check it

Save as optimizely-check.sh, then run bash optimizely-check.sh example.com or pass the project ID: bash optimizely-check.sh 1234567890. Needs bash, curl, grep and sha256sum (Linux, macOS with coreutils, WSL). Messages are Hungarian + English.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# optimizely-check.sh — fertőzött-e az oldalad Optimizely-kódja (2026. november 16-i támadás)?
# Is your site's Optimizely Web snippet carrying the 16 Nov 2026 malware (1688360.cc / webshell.lol)?
# Csak olvas: letölti az oldalt és az Optimizely-snippetet, és IOC-kat keres. Read-only.
#   bash optimizely-check.sh example.com            # főoldal: snippet keresése + CSP-elemzés
#   bash optimizely-check.sh 752092193              # projekt-ID (cdn.optimizely.com/js/<ID>.js)
#   bash optimizely-check.sh https://opt.example.com/js/123.js   # saját domainről kiszolgált snippet
#   DOH=1 bash optimizely-check.sh ...              # ha a saját DNS-szűrőd (Pi-hole, AdGuard) blokkolja az Optimizely-t
# IOC-k forrása / source: https://blog.report-uri.com/worlds-largest-brands-infected-with-malware-via-optimizely/
# MIT license — AikaHub (https://aikahub.com)
set -u
UA="Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/130.0 Safari/537.36"
C=(curl -sS -L -m 30 -A "$UA"); [ "${DOH:-0}" = 1 ] && C+=(--doh-url https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query)
IOC='1688360\.cc|webshell\.lol|linkforge\.cc|5vobauua3ojpklx\.icu|eil786npto9u5bq\.icu|l7bcsnwc7nzr3uo\.icu|je4ft3gn8vxudum\.icu|q1ls1ho9x7wsxlu\.icu|ios-hack\.icu|p55abnw2pnsz0bo\.icu|1y69gy2mdzaltz1\.icu|gm38duxoihbmy5o\.icu|window\._k7|__k7b|02111110|BIGNIAO|aHR0cHM6Ly8xNjg4MzYw|aHR0cHM6Ly93ZWJzaGVsbC5sb2'
BAD_SHA="814a963c0da480e2449d9b6664480156e1cd6d731014117401bf635badec3a0f f7b84b9a94f749f8ced3f0112d0a66894e8bbc3b4aa5592021d1b8976a9bad40"
T=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$T"' EXIT
red() { printf '\033[31m%s\033[0m\n' "$*"; }; grn() { printf '\033[32m%s\033[0m\n' "$*"; }; ylw() { printf '\033[33m%s\033[0m\n' "$*"; }
RC=0

check_js() {  # $1 = snippet URL
  local u=$1 f="$T/s.js" code
  code=$("${C[@]}" -D "$T/h" -o "$f" -w '%{http_code}' "$u" 2>"$T/err") || { ylw "  ! $u: nem tölthető le ($(tail -c 120 "$T/err" | tr -d '\n'))"; [ "${DOH:-0}" = 1 ] || ylw "    Ha a DNS-szűrőd blokkolja: DOH=1 bash $(basename "$0") ..."; [ "$RC" = 0 ] && RC=2; return; }
  [ "$code" = 200 ] || { ylw "  ! $u: HTTP $code"; return; }
  echo "  snippet: $u"
  echo "    méret/size: $(wc -c <"$f") B · Last-Modified: $(grep -i '^last-modified:' "$T/h" | tail -1 | cut -d' ' -f2- | tr -d '\r')"
  local sha; sha=$(sha256sum "$f" | cut -d' ' -f1); echo "    sha256: $sha"
  case " $BAD_SHA " in *" $sha "*) red "    ✘ ISMERT KÁRTEVŐ (track.js) / known malicious track.js hash"; RC=1 ;; esac
  local hits; hits=$(grep -oE "$IOC" "$f" | sort | uniq -c)
  if [ -n "$hits" ]; then red "    ✘ IOC TALÁLAT / IOC FOUND:"; echo "$hits" | sed 's/^/      /'; RC=1
  else grn "    ✔ nincs ismert IOC / no known IOC"; fi
  local a; a=$(grep -o 'atob(' "$f" | wc -l)
  [ "$a" -gt 0 ] && ylw "    ! atob( ×$a — base64-dekódolás; nézd meg a Project JavaScriptet kézzel (a támadás egyik változata így rejtette a címet)"
}

check_csp() {  # $1 = header file
  local csp; csp=$(grep -i '^content-security-policy:' "$1" | tail -1 | cut -d' ' -f2- | tr -d '\r')
  if [ -z "$csp" ]; then ylw "  CSP: nincs (no Content-Security-Policy header) — a kártevő akadály nélkül futott és küldött volna adatot"; return; fi
  echo "  CSP: $(echo "$csp" | cut -c1-160)$( [ ${#csp} -gt 160 ] && echo …)"
  echo "$csp" | grep -q "script-src" || ylw "    ! nincs script-src (default-src-re esik vissza)"
  echo "$csp" | grep -q "'strict-dynamic'" && ylw "    ! 'strict-dynamic': a megbízott snippet által beszúrt scriptet is engedi (így jutott át a track.js)"
  echo "$csp" | grep -q "'unsafe-eval'" && ylw "    ! 'unsafe-eval': az eval-os, beágyazott tartalékváltozat így is fut"
  echo "$csp" | grep -q "connect-src" && grn "    ✔ van connect-src (a kártya/süti-kiküldést ez fogta meg több helyen)" || ylw "    ! nincs connect-src: a lopott adat bárhová kimehet"
}

[ $# -eq 0 ] && { sed -n '2,9p' "$0"; exit 2; }
for arg in "$@"; do
  echo "== $arg"
  if [[ "$arg" =~ ^[0-9]{6,}$ ]]; then check_js "https://cdn.optimizely.com/js/$arg.js"; continue; fi
  url=$arg; [[ "$url" =~ ^https?:// ]] || url="https://$url"
  if [[ "$url" =~ \.js(\?|$) ]]; then check_js "$url"; continue; fi
  code=$("${C[@]}" -D "$T/ph" -o "$T/p.html" -w '%{http_code}' "$url" 2>"$T/err") || { ylw "  ! nem elérhető: $(tail -c 120 "$T/err")"; RC=2; continue; }
  echo "  oldal/page: HTTP $code, $(wc -c <"$T/p.html") B"
  ph=$(grep -oE "$IOC" "$T/p.html" | sort | uniq -c); [ -n "$ph" ] && { red "  ✘ IOC a HTML-ben / in page HTML:"; echo "$ph" | sed 's/^/    /'; RC=1; }
  check_csp "$T/ph"
  host=$(echo "$url" | sed -E 's#^https?://([^/]+).*#\1#')
  mapfile -t S < <(grep -oE '(https?:)?//(cdn(-pci)?\.optimizely\.com|[a-z0-9.-]+)/js/[0-9]{6,}\.js' "$T/p.html" | sed -E 's#^//#https://#' | sort -u)
  if [ ${#S[@]} -eq 0 ]; then
    ylw "  ? Optimizely-snippet nincs a HTML-ben. Ha tag managerrel / hozzájárulás után töltöd, add meg a projekt-ID-t: bash $(basename "$0") <ID>"
    grep -qi optimizely "$T/p.html" && echo "    (az 'optimizely' szó előfordul az oldalon: $(grep -oi optimizely "$T/p.html" | wc -l)×)"
  fi
  for s in "${S[@]}"; do check_js "$s"; done
done
echo; case $RC in 0) grn "Kész: nincs találat. (Clean.)";; 1) red "Kész: TALÁLAT — lásd fent, és nézd meg az Optimizely Project JavaScriptet.";; *) ylw "Kész: nem minden ellenőrzés futott le.";; esac
exit $RC

What it does:

  • finds the Optimizely snippet in the homepage HTML (cdn.optimizely.com, cdn-pci.optimizely.com, or a self-hosted /js/<number>.js);
  • downloads it and prints size, Last-Modified and SHA-256, and compares the hash to the two published track.js hashes;
  • greps for every attacker domain, the window._k7 / __k7b markers, the iOS loader's 02111110 channel code, and the start of the base64 loader (aHR0cHM6Ly8xNjg4MzYw is https://1688360 in base64);
  • warns on any atob( so you can review it by hand;
  • grades your CSP header against what actually stopped (or didn't stop) this attack.

If the snippet isn't in the HTML (loaded via a tag manager or after cookie consent), pass the project ID. You can find it in the Optimizely UI or in your browser's network tab.

Output on real sites

Peacock, one of the affected sites, this afternoon after the clean-up:

== www.peacocktv.com
  oldal/page: HTTP 200, 152025 B
  CSP: default-src https://*.peacocktv.com; form-action https://*.force.com …
    ! 'unsafe-eval': az eval-os, beágyazott tartalékváltozat így is fut
    ✔ van connect-src (a kártya/süti-kiküldést ez fogta meg több helyen)
  snippet: https://cdn-pci.optimizely.com/js/18154240447.js
    méret/size: 336626 B · Last-Modified: Mon, 16 Nov 2026 21:06:21 GMT
    sha256: bb3c2f9e0d0202e45fd204d819703075432afdef022430512a883adf2750762a
    ✔ nincs ismert IOC / no known IOC

The Last-Modified of 21:06 UTC matches the mass clean-up. The unsafe-eval warning means the inline eval fallback would have run even if track.js had been blocked. Optimizely's own snippet is also clean, with a 21:20 UTC date.

One surprise: on my first run cdn.optimizely.com didn't resolve at all, because our home DNS ad blocker answers 0.0.0.0 for it (cdn-pci.optimizely.com got through, though). That's what the DOH=1 switch is for: it resolves through Cloudflare's DNS-over-HTTPS. As a visitor, that kind of DNS filter was protecting us.

What a hit looks like

All real snippets are clean now, so I tested detection with harmless imitations of the loader forms, served from python3 -m http.server on localhost.

The base64 variant (form 2):

== http://127.0.0.1:8899/js/111111111.js
    ✘ IOC TALÁLAT / IOC FOUND:
            1 aHR0cHM6Ly8xNjg4MzYw
    ! atob( ×1 — base64-dekódolás; nézd meg a Project JavaScriptet kézzel (a támadás egyik változata így rejtette a címet)

Kész: TALÁLAT — lásd fent, és nézd meg az Optimizely Project JavaScriptet.

The plain script-tag variant (form 1):

    ✘ IOC TALÁLAT / IOC FOUND:
            1 1688360.cc
            1 window._k7

A clean script that legitimately uses atob( only gets a warning, not an alert. Exit codes: 0 clean, 1 hit, 2 something couldn't be checked, so you can drop it into cron or CI.

If you get a hit:

  1. Review every project's Project JavaScript and every experiment's custom code in Optimizely for 1688360.cc, atob( and anything you didn't write.
  2. Audit and rotate everything that can write to the account: users, API tokens, integrations.
  3. Treat cards entered in your own forms on 16 November as exposed.
  4. Invalidate session tokens kept in non-HttpOnly cookies.
  5. In the EU, check your GDPR Art. 33 breach-notification duty (72 hours). This is information, not legal advice.

CSP lessons

Report URI checked the response headers of 256 affected organisations. Only 24 (15%) blocked the payload completely.

  • Allowlisting cdn.optimizely.com doesn't help: the malware came from there.
  • 'strict-dynamic' let it through, because the trusted snippet inserted it.
  • With 'unsafe-eval', the inline fallback ran even where track.js was blocked (HSBC).
  • A tight connect-src was worth a lot: no card, cookie or screenshot exfiltration. It did not stop address swapping, which happens inside the page.

Visitors: three quick checks

  1. iPhone/iPad: Settings → General → About → iOS Version. According to the kit's own comments, 18.7.3 and 26.3 (and later) are patched.
  2. Crypto: if you pasted an address on 16 November, verify where the funds went. Attacker addresses include BTC 19g9rZcPeiz8rUvyWpTRyXXhPnjsWrc3kW, ETH/EVM 0xC4026b06D82b0F0B363eda0642D61CfbDc17884e and TRON THvs6p56XkUiMkJeSc51cAP64u2RsTYqxa.
  3. Cards: if you paid in a site's own form that day, watch your statements.

Blocklist for Pi-hole / AdGuard 

1688360.cc
webshell.lol
linkforge.cc

eil786npto9u5bq.icu
l7bcsnwc7nzr3uo.icu
je4ft3gn8vxudum.icu
q1ls1ho9x7wsxlu.icu
ios-hack.icu

I queried them over Cloudflare DoH this afternoon. 1688360.cc and webshell.lol return NXDOMAIN (on hold) and eil786npto9u5bq.icu has no A record. The rest still resolve, including the hard-coded fallback C2s (je4ft3gn8vxudum.icu, q1ls1ho9x7wsxlu.icu, ios-hack.icu), so block them now.

Source: Report URI: World's largest brands infected with malware via Optimizely (IOCs, hashes and timeline).
