articles.title: Coding Agents Keep Installing the Old Version of Your Library
articles.description: I work on helping coding agents write better code, and one question keeps coming back. Libraries...
articles.body_html:
I work on helping coding agents write better code, and one question keeps coming back. Libraries change fast: a new major, a renamed package, an API that is gone. Do agents move to the new version as willingly as a developer who reads the release notes, and do they use it as well? If you maintain a library that changed this year, the answer decides what code your users get when they ask an agent for it.

To find out, I took 20 libraries that changed in 2026, most with a new major, a rename or a removed API, and for two weeks gave Claude Code, Codex and Gemini the jobs their users would give them: add "the current" SDK to a small project, upgrade an app to the new major, write code against an API that changed. Each agent did every task several times. A hidden grader checked the code, and a log recorded everything the agent opened.

That came to 34 checks and 433 graded runs. Often the agents did not move. In 31 of the 34 checks they got something wrong in a way the library could fix. Usually the code ran fine on the old version, and the agent told the user it was current.

Asked for "the current version", agents ended on it in 32 of 66 runs

These are the 11 libraries where an agent could install the wrong version: the old package was still latest, the user used the old name, or the old API was still in the package. For the other 9, the new version was what npm or PyPI installed anyway, so the test was the code written against it. Runs on the current version, out of 6 per library: Claude Code, Codex and Gemini, 2 runs each, nothing pointing to the docs.

Below is what happened, in the order an agent meets your library: npm first, then the files on disk, then the docs. The changes that moved the numbers are collected in a checklist at the end.

The test

Each check is one task, worded the way a user would ask, with nothing in the prompt that points to the docs. The task never names the version: "the current version from npm", "upgrade to the current Video.js". Each agent gets a fresh project, web access, full shell and 25 minutes. A script grades the result: which package and version ended up in the code, whether it builds and works against a real or fake server, and whether the agent told the user what it did. A second pass reads the log for what the agent opened: npm, the README, type files, docs pages, llms.txt, skills, MCP tools.

Most checks ran each task twice on each of the three agents, 6 runs per check. Where I tested a fix, I reran the same task with one change switched on: a deprecation through a local registry that behaves like npm, a patched README, a few lines in AGENTS.md. Three experiments compare docs channels with 45 runs each. Small samples like these show big effects only; I say so where it matters.

Where agents decide

Before any docs, an agent asked for "the current version" goes to the package registry. It runs npm view or just npm install, and it sees latest, the README and a deprecation notice if there is one. Most of the wrong choices were made right there, in the first minute.

After that it reads what is on disk: type definitions, the README and docs inside node_modules, error messages from the compiler, the CLI or your server. The docs site comes last, and many runs never got there. llms.txt was opened in 0 of 59 runs where nothing pointed to it.

1. Make latest mean the latest

Prisma 8's CLI was already latest on npm as a release candidate, but @prisma/client@latest still pointed to 7.10.1. Three of six runs chose Prisma 7 on purpose: they saw the CLI and the client on different majors and applied an old, correct rule that the two must match. Only 2 of 6 ended on Prisma 8.

OpenCode's v2 server came with a new SDK, but the old @opencode-ai/sdk was still latest on npm. Three of six runs started on the old one, and its calls to the v2 server got back an HTML page with status 200 instead of an error.

The counterexample is Effect. Its v4 went out under the same name with latest pointing at it, so an agent that installed the obvious package got the new version and the docs that ship with it.

When the new major is the one you want people on, move latest to it. If a companion package can't move yet, say so in its README's first line.

2. Deprecate the old package, then ship one last release that says where to go

Hedera moved its JavaScript SDK to @hiero-ledger/sdk, but the old @hashgraph/sdk was still latest, not deprecated, and its README didn't mention the move (issue). All 6 runs built a correct signed transfer on the old package. None opened the agent skill Hedera had published for exactly this.

I simulated the fix with a local registry that serves the old package as deprecated, exactly as npm would. The same task went from 0 of 6 to 3 of 6 on the new package. The logs show why only half switched. npm view old-pkg prints DEPRECATED at the top, and the runs that used it switched. npm view old-pkg version prints only the number, and npm install prints the warning after the choice is made. One run cut the warning off with | tail -5.

Moss had the same shape after renaming its scope: 3 of 6 on the new @moss-js/moss. A simulated npm deprecate brought it to 4 of 6. Deprecation plus one last release of the old package, whose README opens with "moved, same API, install @moss-js/moss", brought it to 6 of 6. That fix takes about ten minutes. If you want to know whether your own package has this problem, there's a 2-minute read-only check your agent can run.

npm deprecate the old package with the new name in the message, then publish a final patch release of it whose README's first line says where it moved.

3. After a rename, agents use the name the user typed

When the user says the old name, agents follow the user. Context.dev used to be Brand.dev. With "Brand.dev" in the prompt, 4 of 6 runs installed the frozen brand.dev package. With "Context.dev", 6 of 6 used the new SDK.

LadybugDB is the maintained fork of Kùzu, which was archived. Asked to use Kùzu, 6 of 6 runs stayed on the archived kuzu package. A fix in LadybugDB's agent skill got 5 of 6 runs to tell the user Kùzu is archived, though 5 of 6 still installed it. LadybugDB merged that change.

The libraries that kept their name had it easier. Video.js 10 ships as new @videojs/* packages, but the old video.js package now contains a redirect that tells you where the player went. All 6 runs asking for "Video.js, current version" ended on v10 (results).

Keep the package name if you can. If you can't, make the old name lead to the new one everywhere a user's word can land: the old package, its README, your skill, your docs search.

4. Put deprecations where the agent reads them

A deprecation that lives only in JSDoc or on the website doesn't reach the agent that's writing code. Rivet 3.0 deprecated c.state in favor of a new API: 3 of 6 runs used c.state, and none told the user. CopilotKit's v1 API is deprecated in favor of v2: both Gemini runs used v1. Charm's Bubble Tea and Lip Gloss moved to v2 under a new module path: both Gemini runs used v1 and called it current.

Mark renamed and removed APIs @deprecated in the type files with the replacement's name. Keep removed names as stubs for a release so the compiler error points to the right thing, and log a warning at run time that names the replacement.

5. Make error messages name the fix

Kestra 2.0 removed ForEach (now Loop) and the json() function (now fromJson()), and an open issue asks for better errors for exactly these. Over 15 runs with no help, 6 wrote one of them. Each got an error that didn't name the replacement: Invalid type: io.kestra.plugin.core.flow.ForEach, or Function or Macro [json] does not exist. They found the answer by listing the server's plugins, and one run spent 25 minutes, part of it unzipping the server's jar. Claude and Gemini never opened Kestra's 2.0 docs at all, so for them the error message was the only 2.0 documentation they saw.

Mem0's upgrade from 1.x to 2.x removed graph memory from the open-source package. None of four runs told the user that it moved to Mem0's platform, and one Codex run wrote its own Neo4j layer to replace it.

Treat errors for removed things as docs. "ForEach was removed in 2.0, use io.kestra.plugin.core.flow.Loop" costs one line and reaches every agent that hits it.

6. Make the documented path work with nobody at the keyboard

Agents run your commands in a terminal nobody watches. Crash Override's CLI wanted an interactive terminal to produce a report (issue), so 6 of 6 runs had to write their own config file to get one. One Prisma run started init without --yes and waited on a prompt until time ran out.

Docs examples get copied word for word. E2B's docs showed install_cmd and run_cmd for a custom MCP server in a sandbox; all 4 runs that got that far wrote them, and the gateway ignores both. CrewAI's docs offer a prompt to paste into your agent for setup: step 6 failed in 6 of 6 runs (issue).

The default settings shaped results too. Asked to start Arize Phoenix 21 in Docker and send it traces, 6 of 6 runs turned authentication off to get it working, and none used an API key.

Show non-interactive flags in every command, make the CLI work without a terminal, run your docs examples in CI, and make the secure path the one that works on the first try.

7. Ship the docs inside the package

What's in node_modules always matches the installed version and is on disk when the agent hits an error. Video.js ships its full docs in @videojs/html, and the runs read them. Effect ships an AGENTS.md and runnable examples in its package, and every run read them or the source.

Put an upgrade note and the main guides in the tarball, with predictable names (UPGRADE.md, docs/, AGENTS.md).

8. Ten lines beat a docs MCP

Three libraries asked, in public, whether they should build a docs MCP or ship a skill. I ran the same task on each with one channel switched on at a time: nothing, a line pointing to the vendor's llms.txt, the vendor's skill, a docs MCP, and 5 to 13 lines from the vendor's own migration guide in the project's AGENTS.md. That's 9 runs per channel on each library, 135 in all.

The short brief was the only channel with a significant effect, and it was never worse than nothing:

  • Camunda 8.10, picking the current Node client: 4 of 9 with nothing, 9 of 9 with the brief (p = 0.03, results).
  • Video.js 10, upgrading a v8 app: everyone got there, but the brief cut tokens and tool calls by about a third (p ≤ 0.001).
  • Kestra 2.0: no channel made a significant difference. With the brief, the llms.txt pointer or the skill, all 9 first attempts used 2.0 constructs; with nothing or the docs MCP, 7 of 9 did.

The others had specific limits. The docs MCP was called in only 16 of 27 runs, and Codex didn't call it in any of its 9: it had the tools listed and searched the web instead. Kestra's hosted MCP also advertises a login that Codex can't complete, so Codex hides its tools (how to check your own MCP server). Skills were read in 27 of 27 runs and gained nothing measurable; on Kestra the skill was the slowest channel. The llms.txt pointer was followed in 23 of 27 runs and helped exactly as much as the page it led to.

AGENTS.md lives in the user's project, so you can't add lines to it yourself. There are two ways to get them there: your CLI can write those lines during setup (@videojs/cli agents init and Camunda's c8ctl setup already write agent files), or your README can offer the block to copy.

Write the 5 to 15 lines an agent needs for your current version first: the package to install, what was removed, the new names. Ship them in the package and in your CLI's setup. Build an MCP after that, and check that each agent actually calls it.

When none of this applies: the models already know your version

If the models already know your new version, the traps above mostly don't fire. Expo's removed module was still latest and undeprecated, the same trap as Hedera, yet 12 of 12 runs used the replacement: it shipped in 2025, and the models had learned it. Ask the models with tools turned off:

claude -p "From memory, no tools: do you know <package> version <N>? Install command and a 10-line example, or say UNKNOWN." --tools ""

If they answer UNKNOWN, your users' agents will decide from npm, from your errors and from what's on disk, and the sections above are the order to fix them in.

Check your library before the next release

Each line is one change from the sections above, in the order an agent meets your library. The first two are npm commands and take minutes.

  1. Point latest at the version you want people on.
  2. Deprecate a renamed package, and ship one last release whose README says where it moved.
  3. Make the old name lead to the new one everywhere a user might type it.
  4. Mark removed APIs @deprecated in the type files, with the replacement's name.
  5. Name the replacement in the error a removed thing throws.
  6. Make every documented command work with nobody at the keyboard.
  7. Ship an upgrade note and your guides inside the package.
  8. Write 5 to 15 lines for AGENTS.md before you build a docs MCP.

You don't have to go through this list by hand. Two ways to have it checked for your own package:

  • Run the 2-minute npm check. It's read-only, and your agent can do it for you.
  • Ask for a check of your next release. You name the task your users give their agents; I run it on Claude Code, Codex and Gemini and send you what each one did.

Limits

Two or three runs per agent per check: these are examples and big effects, not rates. One task per check, in my wording, on my machine. The fixes for Hedera and Moss are simulations through a local registry; the npm website still showed the old state, though no run opened it. Agents and models change every few weeks, so a check is a snapshot with a date.

The data

Every check here has its prompt, the per-run results, a short step-by-step view of what each agent did and the full logs. Each company has them in a private workspace on Ready for Agents, where they can also connect their own agent to read the results and ask the next question.

articles.title: Building 50 File Tools That Never Upload Your Files: 6 Browser Gotchas
articles.description: What I learned moving image and video processing into the browser with Next.js 16, WebCodecs and...
articles.body_html:
What I learned moving image and video processing into the browser with Next.js 16, WebCodecs and WebAssembly.

I run a video downloader site, and this autumn I added 50 file tools to it: image compression, HEIC to JPG, video to MP3 and GIF, trimming, a ringtone maker, a background remover,
and more. The rule I set was simple: the user's file never touches my server. Everything runs in the browser.

It mostly worked. These are the six things that didn't, and how I fixed them.

  1. Chrome "supports" AVIF export by giving you a PNG

canvas.toBlob(cb, 'image/avif') doesn't throw in Chrome. Per the spec, an unsupported type falls back to PNG, so you get a valid blob with the wrong format. My first version happily saved PNG bytes with a .avif name.

Fix: always check blob.type against what you asked for. When AVIF comes back as something else, I load an AVIF encoder compiled to WebAssembly (jSquash's libavif build) with a dynamic import, so only people who need it download it. Safari can write AVIF natively and never loads it.

Bonus gotcha: the package's normal entry point runs a feature check that embeds WebAssembly as a data URL, and Turbopack refused to bundle it. Importing the single-threaded codec directly avoided that. The threaded build needs cross-origin isolation anyway, which would break third-party scripts.

  1. iOS Safari has a canvas size limit

Safari on iPhone won't create a canvas bigger than 16,777,216 pixels. Go over it, and you don't get an error; you get a blank image. A 48-megapixel iPhone photo is well past that.

Fix: compute the pixel count before drawing, and scale down to fit under the limit. I keep the limit as a named constant so every tool checks it the same way.

  1. Phone videos came out stretched

Videos recorded on phones are often HEVC with rotation metadata. When I resized them to a new aspect ratio with a "fill" fit, they stretched. The fix was to compute the output size from the video's own metadata and use "cover" (crop to fill) rather than "fill" (squash to fill).

The video work itself uses Mediabunny on top of WebCodecs, which made trimming, compressing, and converting surprisingly short to write.

  1. "Compress to 50 KB" is a search problem

JPEG quality doesn't map to file size in any predictable way. To hit a target like 50 KB, I binary-search the quality setting, re-encoding until the result lands just under the target, then shrink the dimensions only if even the lowest acceptable quality is too big. Six or seven encodes usually find it.

  1. Phone testing failed for a silly reason

Uploads worked on desktop and did nothing on my phone. The page loaded, but nothing was interactive. Next.js blocks its dev scripts for origins it doesn't know, and my phone was on a different LAN address than the one in allowedDevOrigins. Reading the machine's addresses at startup fixed it. Hours lost, one line changed.

  1. My CSS was shipped three times

With Next's experimental inlineCss, each page carried its stylesheet in a <style> tag and twice more in the React payload. On top of that, importing one small component from my toolkit's index file pulled in every tool's CSS. Turning inlineCss off and importing the component directly took the homepage from 95 KB to 31 KB gzipped, with the same or better LCP.

Was it worth it?

Yes. No upload means no waiting on mobile data, no storage bill, and nothing to leak. The tools are free at savefrominternet.com/tools. If you've hit other browser gotchas doing this kind of work, I'd like to hear them.

articles.title: File System Access API in a Chrome extension: 8 things that broke
articles.description: I built a Chrome extension that saves ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and other AI chats as Markdown files in...
articles.body_html:
I built a Chrome extension that saves ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and other AI chats as Markdown files in a folder on your computer. You pick a folder (often an Obsidian vault), and every chat becomes one .md file that stays up to date as you keep talking. It's called Chat to Markdown.

The idea fits in one sentence. Making a Manifest V3 extension write to a real folder, reliably, for weeks at a time, took most of the work. This is the list I wish I'd had at the start: what broke, why, and the code that fixed it.

Everything below is about the file side. It applies to any extension that writes to disk, whatever it saves.

Why files and not a database

I want my chats next to my notes, in a format that grep, git and Obsidian already understand, and that will still open in 20 years. chrome.storage or IndexedDB would have been easier, but they lock the data inside the extension. Uninstall it and the chats are gone.

The File System Access API makes the other choice possible. showDirectoryPicker() gives you a handle to a folder the user picked, and you can create, read and write files inside it. Chrome has it. Firefox and Safari don't, so the extension is Chrome only.

The short version:

  1. The service worker can't do the file work. An offscreen document does.
  2. A folder handle can't go in chrome.storage. It goes in IndexedDB.
  3. Permission can disappear after a restart, and only a click brings it back.
  4. The picker refuses some folders, and Brave turns it off.
  5. Chrome rejects file names your OS would accept.
  6. Users edit the files. Only rewrite the part you own.
  7. Obsidian reads more into your Markdown than you wrote.
  8. Version history doesn't need git.

1. Writing files from an MV3 service worker: use an offscreen document

In Manifest V3 the background is a service worker. It has no window, so no folder picker, and in my testing the permission methods on a stored handle weren't usable there either. But the service worker is exactly the part that runs the scheduled sync and needs to write files.

The fix is an offscreen document that acts as a small file server. The worker sends it messages, and it does the reading and writing.

const OFFSCREEN_PATH = 'src/offscreen/offscreen.html';
let creating = null;

async function ensureOffscreen() {
  const contexts = await chrome.runtime.getContexts({
    contextTypes: ['OFFSCREEN_DOCUMENT'],
    documentUrls: [chrome.runtime.getURL(OFFSCREEN_PATH)],
  });
  if (contexts.length) return;
  creating ??= chrome.offscreen
    .createDocument({
      url: OFFSCREEN_PATH,
      reasons: ['BLOBS'],
      justification: 'Write exported chats as Markdown files to the folder the user selected.',
    })
    .finally(() => { creating = null; });
  await creating;
}

const WRITE_TIMEOUT_MS = 90_000;

async function call(type, payload = {}) {
  await ensureOffscreen();
  let clock;
  const gaveUp = new Promise((resolve) => {
    clock = setTimeout(() => resolve(null), WRITE_TIMEOUT_MS);
  });
  const res = await Promise.race([
    chrome.runtime.sendMessage({ target: 'offscreen', type, ...payload }),
    gaveUp,
  ]).finally(() => clearTimeout(clock));
  if (!res) throw new FolderError('unavailable', 'Couldn’t write the file. Try again.');
  if (!res.ok) throw new FolderError(res.code ?? 'error', res.error);
  return res.result;
}

Four details that each cost me a bug:

  • There's no "file system" reason in the offscreen API. BLOBS is the closest fit, and the Web Store accepted it with an honest justification.
  • Share the creation promise. Two saves starting at once would both call createDocument(), and the second one throws because the document already exists.
  • Time out every call. If the offscreen page dies in the middle of a write, sendMessage can just hang, and every save after it waits in line forever. After 90 seconds the call fails with a message a person can act on.
  • Messages are JSON. Images and files from a chat travel as base64, built in 32 KB chunks. Spreading a whole 5 MB Uint8Array into String.fromCharCode(...bytes) overflows the call stack.

The offscreen side is just a table of operations:

import * as fs from '../storage/fs-ops.js';

const operations = {
  check: () => fs.check(),
  read: ({ path }) => fs.read(path),
  write: ({ path, content }) => fs.write(path, content),
  writeBytes: ({ path, data }) => fs.writeBytes(path, data),
  exists: ({ path }) => fs.exists(path),
  remove: ({ path }) => fs.remove(path),
  list: ({ path }) => fs.list(path),
};

chrome.runtime.onMessage.addListener((msg, _sender, sendResponse) => {
  if (msg?.target !== 'offscreen') return false;
  const op = operations[msg.type];
  if (!op) return false;
  Promise.resolve()
    .then(() => op(msg))
    .then(
      (result) => sendResponse({ ok: true, result }),
      (err) => sendResponse({ ok: false, code: err.code ?? err.name, error: err.message }),
    );
  return true; // keeps the channel open for the async answer
});

Extension pages (the reader, the import page) can use the handle directly, without the round trip. So there are two objects with the same shape, workerIo and pageIo, and the save code takes either one. The same function saves a chat from a background sync and from an import running in a tab.

2. Storing a FileSystemDirectoryHandle: IndexedDB, not chrome.storage

The user picks a folder once. You need that handle again tomorrow, in a different context, after the service worker has been killed and restarted a hundred times.

chrome.storage only holds JSON, and a handle isn't JSON. IndexedDB uses structured cloning, which handles support. Every page of an extension shares one origin (chrome-extension://<id>), so the welcome page that saves the handle and the offscreen document that uses it see the same database.

function openDb() {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const req = indexedDB.open('chattomarkdown', 1);
    req.onupgradeneeded = () => req.result.createObjectStore('handles');
    req.onsuccess = () => resolve(req.result);
    req.onerror = () => reject(req.error);
  });
}

async function run(mode, op) {
  const db = await openDb();
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const tx = db.transaction('handles', mode);
    const req = op(tx.objectStore('handles'));
    tx.oncomplete = () => { db.close(); resolve(req.result); };
    tx.onerror = () => { db.close(); reject(tx.error); };
  });
}

export const loadRootHandle = () => run('readonly', (s) => s.get('root'));
export const saveRootHandle = (h) => run('readwrite', (s) => s.put(h, 'root'));

3. Keeping folder permission after a Chrome restart

For years, permission to a picked folder lasted only until the browser closed. Chrome 122 added persistent permissions: the prompt now offers Allow on every visit. If the user picks Allow this time instead, then after a restart queryPermission() returns 'prompt'.

The catch: requestPermission() needs a user gesture. A background sync at 3 a.m. can't ask. So I stopped treating lost permission as an error and gave it its own state:

  • Before each sync, check the permission. If it isn't 'granted', skip the sync instead of failing halfway.
  • Put a red ! on the toolbar icon so the user notices.
  • Show an Allow access button in the popup and in Settings. Its click handler is the gesture: 
$('#reconnect').addEventListener('click', async () => {
  const handle = await loadRootHandle();
  if (handle && (await handle.requestPermission({ mode: 'readwrite' })) === 'granted') {
    toast('Access restored');
    syncNow();
  }
});

The setup screen also tells people to choose Allow on every visit. That one line of text prevents most of these cases.

4. showDirectoryPicker errors: when the picker says no

Two cases left users looking at a button that did nothing.

Chrome refuses some folders. Documents, Desktop and Downloads themselves can't be picked ("contains system files"), only folders inside them. My picker opened in Documents, so that was the first thing people tried. Chrome shows its own dialog, and when the user closes it your code gets an AbortError, the same as a plain cancel. Now a cancel shows a note that explains this and suggests clicking New folder in the picker.

Brave ships with the API turned off. window.showDirectoryPicker is simply undefined, so the click threw "is not a function". Now the extension checks for it before showing the button and, in Brave, links to the flag that turns it on.

export const canPickFolder = () => typeof window.showDirectoryPicker === 'function';
const isBrave = () => Boolean(navigator.brave);

export async function pickFolder() {
  if (!canPickFolder()) throw Object.assign(new Error('Folder access is off'), { name: 'FolderUnsupported' });
  // `id` makes the picker remember where it was last time, per id.
  return window.showDirectoryPicker({ id: 'chattomarkdown', mode: 'readwrite', startIn: 'documents' });
}

5. The "Name is not allowed" error

Chat titles become file names, and chat titles contain anything. Chrome's file system access is stricter than macOS or Windows, and it fails with Name is not allowed on names your OS would take. These all came from real chats:

  • Emoji built with a zero-width joiner, like 👨‍💻. The joiner is a format character (\p{Cf}), and Chrome rejects it.
  • A ~ anywhere in the name.
  • Half an emoji. Cut a title at 80 characters and you can split a surrogate pair.
  • Windows device names, like CON or nul.md. Chrome refuses them, and a vault made on a Mac often syncs to a Windows PC later anyway.
  • Attachments ending in .lnk or .local. These are saved as .bin now.
  • Long names in Chinese, Japanese or Korean. Most file systems allow 255 bytes, not 255 characters. 120 characters of Japanese is 360 bytes of UTF-8. 
const ILLEGAL = /[\\/:*?"<>|#^[\]~\p{Cc}]/gu;
const INVISIBLE = /[\p{Cf}\p{Cs}\p{Noncharacter_Code_Point}]/gu;
const RESERVED = /^(?:con|prn|aux|nul|com[1-9]|lpt[1-9]|clock\$)(?:\.|$)|^(?:desktop\.ini|thumbs\.db)$/i;

export function cleanText(value) {
  return String(value ?? '')
    .replace(INVISIBLE, '')
    .replace(ILLEGAL, ' ')
    .replace(/\s+/g, ' ')
    .trim()
    .replace(/^\.+/, '')
    .replace(/[. ]+$/, '');
}

const utf8 = new TextEncoder();

// At most `max` UTF-16 units (never half an emoji) and `maxBytes` of UTF-8.
export function clip(text, max, maxBytes = 240) {
  let out = text.length <= max ? text : text.slice(0, max).replace(/[\uD800-\uDBFF]$/, '');
  if (utf8.encode(out).length > maxBytes) {
    const chars = [...out];
    while (chars.length && utf8.encode(chars.join('')).length > maxBytes) chars.pop();
    out = chars.join('');
  }
  return out === text ? text : out.replace(/[. ]+$/, '');
}

#, ^, [ and ] are in that list for a different reason: they break Obsidian links. Every bad title I find goes into the unit tests as a fixture.

6. People edit the files: only rewrite what you own

Once a chat is a note, people treat it like one. They add a summary at the top, a status: read property, a link to a project note. Then they continue the chat, and the next sync must update the file without wiping any of that.

The generated part of each file sits between two HTML comments. They're invisible in Obsidian's reading view and in most Markdown previews:

---
title: "Lisbon food trip"
source: "ChatGPT"
tags: [ai-chat, chatgpt]
status: read
---

My summary: Day 2 is the one to book ahead.

<!-- chattomarkdown:start · updated automatically on sync; write your own notes above or below this block -->
# Lisbon food trip

## You

Plan 3 days of eating in Lisbon.

## ChatGPT

Day 1 starts at Time Out Market.
<!-- chattomarkdown:end -->

On every sync, only the text between the markers is replaced. The frontmatter is merged key by key: keys the extension owns (title, url, updated and so on) are rewritten, tags is written only when the file is created, and keys the user added are never touched. If someone deletes the markers, the file is theirs, and the extension never writes to it again.

export function mergeDocument(existing, { fields, body }) {
  const block = buildBlock(body);
  if (existing == null) {
    return { status: 'created', content: `${serializeFrontmatter(fields)}\n${block}\n` };
  }
  const text = existing.replace(/\r\n/g, '\n');
  const { entries, rest } = parseFrontmatter(text);
  const start = rest.indexOf(START_MARK);
  const end = rest.indexOf(END_MARK);
  if (start === -1 || end === -1 || end < start) return { status: 'detached', content: null };

  const content =
    mergeFrontmatter(entries, fields) + rest.slice(0, start) + block + rest.slice(end + END_MARK.length);
  return { status: content === text ? 'unchanged' : 'updated', content };
}

The bug I didn't see coming: someone pasted a saved note into a new chat. Now the chat text itself contained the markers. On the next sync, indexOf found the pasted end marker first, the block ended early, and the file grew on every sync. The fix is a zero-width space inside any marker that appears in the chat text, so it still reads the same but never matches:

const MARK_IN_BODY = /<!--(\s*chattomarkdown:(?:start|end))/g;
const buildBlock = (body) =>
  `${START_COMMENT}\n${body.trim().replace(MARK_IN_BODY, '<!--\u200b$1')}\n${END_MARK}`;

7. Obsidian reads more into your Markdown than you wrote

Valid Markdown isn't enough. I copied a real vault with 677 saved chats and opened it in Obsidian 1.15. Here's what I found:

  • 136 tags came from chat text. #fyp from a drafted social post, #0B1017 from a stylesheet. Obsidian turns any #word into a tag, so the tag pane filled with junk. Now #word is saved as \#word, except in code, links and HTML. A heading like "Learning C#" keeps its #.
  • 965 headings in answers sat at the same level as the speakers. A ## Summary inside a reply looked like a new turn in the outline. Now every heading in a message is pushed down so it starts at ###, and ## You and ## ChatGPT are the only level-2 headings. The outline follows the chat turn by turn.
  • Dollar signs became math. A question about nginx with $host$request_uri rendered as a formula. In the user's own messages, dollars that would pair up into a formula are escaped unless they hold one.
  • Dates were plain text. created and updated didn't sort or filter as dates, because Obsidian reads property types from .obsidian/types.json.

That last fix needs care, because types.json is the user's file too. The extension adds only the types that are missing, never changes one that's already set, and leaves a file it can't parse alone:

const types = data.types ?? {};
const missing = keys.filter((key) => !Object.hasOwn(types, key));
if (!missing.length) return 'unchanged';
const next = { ...data, types: { ...types, ...Object.fromEntries(missing.map((k) => [k, 'datetime'])) } };
await io.write('.obsidian/types.json', JSON.stringify(next, null, 2)); // two spaces, as Obsidian writes it

If you write Markdown for Obsidian users, test in a real vault with real, messy data. Sample files hide all of these.

8. Version history without git

Chats change. People continue them, regenerate answers, rename them, delete them on the site. I wanted a git-style log for each chat without asking anyone to install git.

Each chat gets one JSON file in a hidden folder: .chattomarkdown/history/<service>/<id>.json. Obsidian and Finder don't show dot folders, and keying by chat id means renaming or moving the note doesn't break its history.

The file holds the newest text in full, plus, for each older version, a patch that turns it back into the version before. That's the same trick as RCS's reverse deltas. It's cheap here because a continued chat only changes at the end:

  • The diff is Myers' O(ND) algorithm, run only on the middle part after the common start and end are set aside. For a continued chat that middle part is tiny.
  • Lines are mapped to small integers first, so comparing them is cheap.
  • History stops at 100 versions or 4 million characters, whichever comes first.
  • If the user edited the file between two syncs, their edit is kept as its own "edited" version, so the next sync can't silently erase it from history.

One rule above all the others: history must never stop a chat from saving. The function that records a change catches everything. A broken history file costs you a log entry. A failed save costs you a chat.

What I'd tell someone starting an extension that writes files

  • Decide early which part of each file you own, and never touch the rest.
  • Treat permission as a state that can change at any time, with UI for each state, not an error path.
  • Keep the worst file names you can find as test fixtures. Emoji, CJK, Windows device names, a lone ~.
  • Test against the app people will open the files in, with a copy of real data.
  • Put a timeout on anything that crosses a process boundary.

If you want your own AI chats as files, Chat to Markdown is free for 10 chats, with no account. The full file format is documented line by line, and I wrote up how I organise hundreds of AI chats in Obsidian with properties and Dataview.

How do you keep your AI chats today? Exports, copy and paste, or not at all? And if you've shipped an extension that writes to disk, I'd like to hear what broke for you. I'll answer questions about the offscreen setup in the comments.

articles.title: How I Built an Open-Source AI Browser Extension That Actually Executes Tasks
articles.description: A few months ago I got frustrated with AI tools that could talk about doing things but couldn't...
articles.body_html:
A few months ago I got frustrated with AI tools that could talk about doing things but couldn't actually do them. So I built Cosmos: an open-source Chrome extension where you describe a goal in plain English and watch it get done.

Today I'm open-sourcing it. Here's what it does, how it works, and what I learned building it.

What Cosmos Does

You type a goal — "extract all product prices from this page as JSON" or "fill in this form with my saved details" — and Cosmos:

  1. Reads the live DOM (not a screenshot — the actual structured page)
  2. Sends that + your goal to an LLM and gets back a step-by-step plan
  3. Validates the plan against a strict Zod schema (bad LLM output is rejected, not executed)
  4. Executes each step: click, type, scroll, navigate, extract data
  5. Streams every step back to you live in a side panel

It also remembers. Every run updates a 5-layer memory system so Cosmos gets better at the sites you use most.

The Tech Stack

  • Chrome MV3 — service worker background, content scripts, Side Panel API
  • React 18 + Zustand — the popup/sidepanel UI
  • Dexie (IndexedDB) — the memory layers
  • Zod — plan output validation
  • Vite + Tailwind CSS v3 — build and styling
  • Any OpenAI-compatible API — OpenRouter, Groq, or self-hosted OmniRoute

The Architecture Decision I'm Most Proud Of

Most extension AIs do this:

user types goal → background sends request → content script acts → done

That doesn't work for multi-step tasks. You need to stream progress back, handle cancellation, and let the user approve risky steps mid-flight.

So Cosmos uses a long-lived port (chrome.runtime.connect) between the popup and the background service worker. The orchestrator streams typed events over that port:

type ChatStreamEvent =
  | { kind: "text_chunk"; delta: string }
  | { kind: "status"; stepId: string; status: StepStatus }
  | { kind: "timeline"; steps: PlanStep[] }
  | { kind: "memory_insight"; note: string }
  | { kind: "screenshot_capture"; stepId: string; dataUrl: string }
  | { kind: "token_usage"; estimatedTokens: number }
  | { kind: "done"; success: boolean }
  | { kind: "error"; message: string }

The Zustand store in the popup handles these events and updates the UI. No polling, no request/response ping-pong — just a stream.

The 5-Layer Memory System

The thing that makes Cosmos genuinely useful after a few runs is memory. Each layer serves a different purpose:

Layer What it stores Lifetime
Session Current goal, execution state, active tab Until popup closes
User Preferences, frequent sites, saved form data Persistent
Website Per-domain selector notes, structure hints Persistent
Workflow Named step sequences with usage/success stats Persistent
Failure What went wrong, what recovery worked Persistent

Before every task, Cosmos queries all five layers. The planner prompt includes relevant workflow steps and known failure recovery strategies — so it doesn't repeat mistakes.

The LLM Planner

The planner is the most interesting part to get right. It has three jobs:

  1. Build the prompt — goal + page snapshot (interactive elements, text, forms, tables) + relevant memory + variable context from prior steps
  2. Call the LLM — streamed, so the UI can show typing
  3. Validate the response — Zod schema, before any action runs

The schema enforcement is strict. If the LLM hallucinates an action type that doesn't exist, the whole plan is rejected and the user gets a clear error — not a half-executed mess.

const ActionTypeSchema = z.enum([
  "click", "type", "scroll", "navigate", "select",
  "assert", "extract", "wait",
  "open_tab", "close_tab", "switch_tab",
  "read_clipboard", "write_clipboard",
]);

What I Would Do Differently

1. Start with the port architecture from day one.
I initially tried request/response messaging for everything. Switching to a long-lived port mid-way was painful but completely necessary for streaming.

2. The DOM reader is the most important module.
Everything downstream — the planner, the browser controller — depends on the quality of the page snapshot. I spent more time on the DOM reader than anything else and it was worth it. Giving every interactive element a stable data-cosmos-id attribute before the snapshot is what makes the action executor reliable.

3. Plan validation saves you from yourself.
Early on I skipped validation to move fast. The first time the LLM returned malformed JSON and the extension tried to execute it, I added Zod immediately. It's never been an issue since.

What's Next

The repo is live and open source under MIT:

https://github.com/Cosmos-Agentic-AI/Cosmos_browser_extension

The ROADMAP has a full list of what's planned, including items tagged good first issue if you want to contribute.

The biggest things I want help with:

  • Firefox support (MV2 compatibility)
  • More AI providers (Anthropic Claude, Gemini, Ollama)
  • Real embedding-based memory retrieval

If you build something with it or find a bug, open an issue. I read everything.

Star the repo if this was useful: github.com/Cosmos-Agentic-AI/Cosmos_browser_extension
